decks.title: Anterior Eye: slit lamp recap
decks.summary: Prof Naroo's recap of the slit lamp: GOC outcomes, setting up the biomicroscope (with and without a focusing rod), every illumination method with its set-up and uses, coupled vs decoupled viewing, fluorescein assessment, RGP fitting patterns, lid eversion and Van Herick grading.
takeaways: Set-up order matters: clean, table height, focus eyepieces (rod or closed eyelid), IPD, patient position, chinrest.
Conical beam is medium magnification at 45–60° in a darkened room (Tyndall effect).
Indirect, retro-illumination and sclerotic scatter need the observation system decoupled.
Specular reflection is seen through one eyepiece only; reduce the angle for deeper structures.
Tangential illumination (about 70°) is for the iris.
Van Herick (Aston grading): 4 = 1:1 wide open, 3 = 1:½ open, 2 = 1:¼ narrow, 1 = <¼ dangerously narrow.

outline.title: Anterior Eye: slit lamp recap
points: Prof Shehzad Naroo, Professor of Investigative Ophthalmology and Optometry.

outline.title: GOC outcomes

outline.title: Setting up the biomicroscope
points: Clean headrest and chinrest; adjust table height.
With a focusing rod: focus eyepieces → set IPD → position patient → adjust chinrest.
Without a rod: position patient → adjust chinrest → focus eyepieces → set IPD.

outline.title: Focusing the eyepieces (with rod)
points: Turn each eyepiece anticlockwise to maximum plus.
Put the focusing rod at the shared axis of illumination and observation.
Narrow the slit; turn each eyepiece until the slit is just in focus.

outline.title: Focusing the eyepieces (no rod)
points: Patient in place with eyes closed; rotate the illumination arm.
Against movement → move the slit lamp closer; with movement → move it further away.
No movement → the eyelid is at the shared focus; focus the eyepieces on the slit.

outline.title: Slit lamp techniques
points: Illumination: diffuse, direct, indirect, retro, sclerotic scatter, specular reflection.
Viewing: optic section, conical beam, parallelepiped, Van Herick, fluorescein staining, everted lids.

outline.title: Diffuse illumination
points: Use a diffuser (flip-up, reversed mirror — even a tissue).
Low magnification (typically 6× or 10×), wide beam.
General view of the eye and adnexa.

outline.title: Direct: optic section
points: Thin beam, vary the angle, low to high magnification.
Shows depth: AC depth; localises nerve fibres, blood vessels, infiltrates and cataracts.

outline.title: Direct: parallelepiped
points: Broader beam lights a block of cornea, low to high magnification.
Corneal nerve fibres, punctate keratitis.

outline.title: Direct: conical beam
points: Small circular beam, narrow and short, 45–60°, medium magnification.
Darkened room so the pupil is a dark background (Tyndall effect).
AC inflammatory cells and flare.

outline.title: Indirect illumination
points: As direct, but look to the side of the beam — the direct beam can bleach defects from view.
Decouple to focus the observation system beside the beam.
Epithelial vesicles and erosions, iris pathology and sphincter, limbal vessels, corneal tissue changes.

outline.title: Coupled vs decoupled
points: Photos comparing the two set-ups (coupled: illumination and observation focused together; decoupled: offset).

outline.title: Retro-illumination
points: Light reflected from the iris or fundus back-lights the cornea.
Moderately wide beam, decoupled, medium to high magnification.
Microcysts (appear reversed), vacuoles, lens opacities, CL deposits, vascularisation.

outline.title: Specular reflection
points: Angle of incidence = angle of observation; the tear film acts as a mirror (Purkinje image).
Medium to high magnification; focus on the area, then swing the beam until the reflection appears.
Visible through one eyepiece only; reduce the angle for deeper structures.
Tear film debris and flow, endothelium, crystalline lens 'orange peel'.

outline.title: Sclerotic scatter
points: 1–1.5 mm slit on the limbus; total internal reflection through the cornea.
Observation decoupled and focused on the cornea, low magnification; halo of light in a darkened room.
Corneal scars, oedema and foreign bodies.

outline.title: Tangential illumination
points: Illumination and observation almost at right angles (about 70°).
Low to medium magnification, wide beam.
Iris freckles, tumours, general integrity of cornea and iris.

outline.title: Fluorescein assessment
points: Broad beam, blue light with a yellow filter.
Conjunctiva, cornea and TBUT.
Adding the yellow (Wratten) filter makes differences in tear thickness much easier to see.

outline.title: RGP fitting patterns
points: Example fluorescein patterns for RGP lenses (see the RGP fitting topic).

outline.title: Lid eversion
points: Prepare the slit lamp first; cotton bud or finger.
Push lashes apart, hold the upper lashes and pull down, bud at the top of the tarsal plate.
Down-and-round motion; afterwards the patient blinks to straighten the lid.
Look with white light and blue light.

outline.title: Van Herick technique
points: Low magnification optic section, about 60° between illumination and observation (straight ahead).
Compare corneal width with AC depth.
Grade 4: 1:1 wide open; grade 3: 1:½ open; grade 2: 1:¼ narrow; grade 1: <¼ dangerously narrow.

outline.title: Learning outcomes for this lecture
points: CL practice in the UK and globally; why fit CLs; history and symptoms; key baseline measurements. (Acknowledges Prof James Wolffsohn.)

outline.title: Why contact lenses?
points: More natural vision; no frames slipping or marking; better appearance and magnification (especially for myopes); wider field.
Optics stay aligned with the eye; no fogging; fewer rain and perspiration problems.
Better for anisometropia and irregular astigmatism; good for sport, goggles, cameras and microscopes.
UV protection, cosmetic benefits and myopia control.

outline.title: History of contact lenses
points: Early ideas (Celsus, Da Vinci, Descartes 1637, de la Hire 1685) don't really describe CLs.
Thomas Young (1801) and John Herschel (1827) deserve more credit — Herschel suggested a jelly-filled capsule or a corneal mould for irregular corneas.
Fick (moulded lenses), Kalt (lenses change corneal shape), Müller (−14 D, corrected himself, ~30 min wear), Zeiss (lathe-cut lenses, first trial sets).

outline.title: History of CL (timeline images)
points: Image-only slides — see the original deck.

outline.title: CL practice today
points: Optical correction, myopia control, therapeutic/medical, aesthetic, specialist (drug delivery, scleral lenses).
Increasing silicone hydrogel wear.
Spherical/toric, single vision/multifocal; GP corneal or scleral; soft hydrogel or silicone hydrogel; daily disposable, planned replacement, reusable; ortho-K.

outline.title: History taking
points: Patient preferences: reason for CLs, current lens/modality/brand, years of wear, hours per day, care solution, quality-of-life benefits.
Lifestyle: age, recreation, occupation/hobbies, home and work environment, digital devices.
Health: general health and medicines, ocular health/surgery/medicines, family history, allergies.
Refractive state: non-astigmatic, astigmatic, presbyopic, paediatric/myopia.

outline.title: Symptoms (SOCRATES)
points: Site, onset, character (flare/glare, blur; burning, gritty, itchy, watery, tired), timing, exacerbating/relieving factors (including with CLs), severity.

outline.title: Conditions to look out for
points: Allergy/hay fever, diabetes, systemic inflammatory disease (e.g. sarcoidosis), thyroid eye disease, skin conditions linked to blepharitis, previous eye surgery — onset, type, control, family history.

outline.title: Medication and contact lens wear
points: Systemic drugs can depress blinking, reduce tear volume and cause dryness, irritation, blur or intolerance (e.g. antihistamines, antidepressants, diuretics, tranquillisers, muscle relaxants, alcohol).
Some can increase corneal sensitivity or cause corneal oedema.
Topical drugs and preservatives can be absorbed and retained by lenses, especially hydrogels.

outline.title: Contraindications
points: Low refractive error, horizontal prism, infection/inflammation, recurrent corneal erosion, diabetes, sinus and allergy problems, sensitive or dry eyes/poor blinking, acne rosacea/seborrhoeic conditions, adverse environments.

outline.title: (Image-only slide)

outline.title: Prior to fitting
points: Counsel and document: lens type, modality, care regimen, risks, time to full-time wear, possible visual compromise/discomfort, what to do in an emergency, costs.

outline.title: Baseline measurements
points: HVID, pupil diameter (room and dim light), K readings/topography, corneal shape/scleral dimensions if needed.
HVID methods: topographer, autorefractor, slit lamp reticule, aberrometer, PD ruler; 10–14 mm, average 11.7 mm.
Pupils with a ruler (or Burton lamp): room (photopic) and dim (scotopic). VPA is rarely used now.

outline.title: Today's clinic (week 1 practical)
points: Why wear contact lenses — who to talk to about the benefits.
Hygiene: wash hands well and dry them before handling lenses.

Record history and symptoms on the record card: reason for wear and modality, previous CL wear, ocular history, general health and meds (diabetes, glaucoma, hypertension, dry eyes, allergies), family history.
Baseline measures: what to measure and how.

outline.title: Summary
points: CL practice in the UK and globally, history of CLs, why fit CLs and contraindications, history and symptoms, baseline measurements (HVID and pupil size).

decks.title: Reflection for healthcare professionals
decks.summary: What reflective practice is, why the GOC expects it for your whole career, the models you can use (What? So what? Now what? and Gibbs' cycle), and what good academic reflective writing looks like.
takeaways: Reflection turns experience into learning; critical reflection goes past describing to analysing.
Two models to know: Driscoll / Rolfe (What? So what? Now what?) and Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988).
Academic reflection is structured and formal, not a diary: description is only the foundation.
CPD reflections must be anonymised: nothing that identifies a patient or practitioner.

outline.title: Aims and GOC outcomes
points: Discuss the purpose of reflective practice, know models you can use, and assess your own learning needs.
Links to GOC outcomes 7.4 (critical reflection on your own development) and 5.1 (recognising when performance puts people at risk).

outline.title: What reflective practice is
points: GOC definition: thinking analytically about your experiences to gain insight and improve the care you give.
Critical reflection moves from descriptive to analytical: evaluate current practice, think what is desirable, consider what is possible, and form new understanding that changes what you do.

outline.title: Models of reflection
points: Driscoll (2000) / Rolfe et al. (2001): What? So what? Now what?
Gibbs (1988) reflective cycle: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.

outline.title: Misconceptions about reflective writing
points: It is not just description, not a personal diary, and not marked on self-disclosure or on flattering the course.
Show how you learned something, what it means for you and how you will use it; keep it appropriate for the reader.

outline.title: Benefits
points: Embeds good practice and is linked to better quality of care.
Assures the public that professionals keep learning; improves individuals, teams and processes.

outline.title: Your CPD reflections
points: Consider what you expected, what you learned, and whether and how you will apply it.
Prompt questions: what happened, what did you take away, what would you do differently, what quick changes can you make, and how will you close longer-term gaps?

decks.title: Multifocal lenses part 1: bifocals and trifocals
decks.summary: Why presbyopes need an addition, how bifocals developed from the Franklin split to today's solid plastic D28, bifocal terminology and fitting, how additions are measured, and when a trifocal fills the gap in an older presbyope's range.
takeaways: Addition = near prescription minus distance prescription (transpose first so both are in the same cyl form).
Most bifocals you meet are solid, plastic, front-surface D28s.
Optically best to worst: split, E-style, prism-controlled, D-segment, round, fused, seamless. Cosmetically it is close to the reverse.
Fit the segment top at the lower limbus for general use; keep a happy wearer's segment position the same.
Measure the add on the surface carrying the segment: front-surface segments with front vertex power, back-surface segments with back vertex power.

outline.title: Why an addition is needed
points: Presbyopia makes the eye an increasingly fixed-focus system; a near object needs extra positive power the eye can no longer supply.
Add = near Rx − distance Rx. Example: distance +2.00 DS, near +5.00 DS gives a +3.00 add; distance −6.00, near −5.00 gives +1.00.
If distance and near are written in different cyl forms, transpose one before working out the add.

outline.title: Bifocal designs and development
points: Shapes: round (downcurve), D-segment, C-segment (curved top), E-style. The larger portion is the major portion.

Franklin split, then cemented, cement Kryptok, fused (glass only, high-index segment in a depression curve), solid (one piece; plastic solids are the commonest today), seamless (blended, poor optics, made obsolete by PPLs) and the one-piece E-style 'Executive'.

outline.title: Current use and choosing a segment
points: Availability: D28 and D35 (D40 specialist); R22 to R45; C28.
The ideal bifocal matches single-vision optics and looks invisible; only the split bifocal meets the optical ideal, and every other design is a compromise.
Choice depends on prescription (round better for plus, D better for minus), field of view, occupation, appearance, weight, material availability and what the patient wore before.

outline.title: Terminology and fitting
points: Segment top position (STP) is measured from the horizontal centre line; segment drop is measured from the distance optical centre; geometric inset is measured from the distance centration point.
If the lens is glazed with the optical centre on the HCL, segment drop and STP have the same value.
Fit segment top level with the lower limbus for general use (some guides say 2 mm below for D-segs); higher for heavy close work, lower for occasional close work. Always state above or below HCL.

outline.title: Semi-finished blanks and measuring additions
points: A blank marked '4-250' has a +4.00 front curve and a +2.50 add; the back surface is worked to give the prescription, and prism can be worked to place the optical centre.
The add is F near − F distance measured on the surface that carries the segment. Distance power is always given as back vertex power.
Measuring a front-surface add with back vertex power over-reads it, most on thick lenses with steep front curves (e.g. a nominal 3.00 add reading 3.32).

outline.title: Trifocals
points: A young presbyope (3 D accommodation, +1.00 add) has overlapping distance and near ranges; an older presbyope (0.75 D, +2.50 add) is left with a blurred gap from 40 cm to 133 cm.
An intermediate add of 50–60% of the near add (e.g. +1.50) gives clear vision from about 44 to 67 cm and narrows that gap.
Fit the top of the intermediate segment higher: the bottom of the pupil is a good starting point.

decks.title: Binocular balancing, binocular addition and binocular refraction (plus week 6 assessment brief)
decks.file: Mgmt_AaM_3_Binocular balancing, binocular addition and binocular refraction plus assessment brief_AS.pptx
decks.summary: The brief for the week 6 retinoscopy and subjective assessment, then three techniques: binocular balancing by monocular fogging, binocular addition, and binocular subjective refraction, with how to record each.
takeaways: Binocular balancing balances accommodation between the eyes; it does not equalise vision.
Monocular fogging (modified Humphriss): fog one eye with about +0.75 DS to roughly 6/12, then find the sphere for best VA in the other eye.
Final Rx = subjective + binocular balance + binocular addition.
Binocular refraction needs no balance afterwards and avoids the problems occlusion causes (latent nystagmus, cyclophoria, pupil dilation).
Week 6 assessment: 15 minutes, ret and subjective on one eye with a dummy lens, 19 marks, pass 10/19, worth 3%.

outline.title: Week 6 assessment brief
points: 15 minutes for retinoscopy and subjective refraction on one eye of a student patient wearing a dummy lens; keep a clinical record and give clear instructions.
Worth 3% of stage 2. Maximum 19 marks, pass mark 10/19; below that means a referred assessment.
Arrive at least 10 minutes early with your equipment (blu-tak is recommended to hold the dummy lens); missing your slot scores 0. No contact lenses when you are the patient.

outline.title: Why balance, and the techniques
points: Occlusion during monocular refraction can cause proximal accommodation; an imbalance in the final Rx may cause asthenopia.

Techniques: monocular fogging (preferred with a trial frame), prism-dissociated blur balance (preferred with a phoropter), Humphriss immediate contrast, and Turville infinite balance (cumbersome, needs a septum).

outline.title: Monocular fogging step by step
points: Fogging suppresses central vision in one eye but keeps peripheral fusion, so both eyes work together with accommodation balanced and relaxed.
After ret and monocular subjective on both eyes, keep the lenses in. Fog the left eye with about +0.75 DS; check it reads about 6/12 (add more plus if not).

In the right eye add +0.25 DS: if clearer or the same keep adding until acuity first blurs. Then try −0.25 DS: only accept it if letters are clearer, not just smaller and blacker. Repeat with the right eye fogged.

outline.title: Binocular addition
points: Often unnecessary because fogging has already relaxed accommodation, but useful for patients who need maximum plus, such as low hyperopes with near symptoms.
Remove the fog, add +0.25 DS to both eyes while it is clearer or the same, and stop when acuity first blurs. If ret suggests latent hyperopia, start with +1.00 DS both eyes and reduce.
Caution: some patients prefer slightly less plus, and a 6 m chart is at a dioptric distance of −0.16 D.

outline.title: Binocular subjective refraction
points: Advantages: accommodation stays balanced throughout (good for hyperopia, pseudomyopia, antimetropia); no occlusion, so no pupil dilation, latent nystagmus or cyclophoria effects; slightly quicker.
Disadvantages: hard with a strongly dominant eye, and only works if the starting point is close to the final result.
Procedure: ret both eyes, fog the left with +0.75 DS (check 6/12), JCC the right, swap, remove the fog, then binocular addition if needed. No separate balance.

outline.title: Recording
points: Record ret, subjective and VA for each eye, the +1.00 DS check test, the binocular balance result for each eye, the binocular addition and binocular VA.
For binocular refraction write 'Bin. balance: N/A (bin refraction)'. Write clearly and in an organised way.

decks.title: The retina, the LGN and visual pathways
decks.summary: From light to the cortex: the visible spectrum, how the retina is wired, rods and cones, M-, P- and K-cells, convergence, the blind spot, and the primary visual pathway through the LGN to V1.
takeaways: Light is not coloured: hue is the experience that goes with wavelength, and the colour code is the pattern of activity across three cone classes.
The retina is wired back to front: light crosses the ganglion cells and interneurons before it reaches the receptors.
Convergence averages 100:1. Low in the fovea (resolution), high in the periphery (sensitivity).
P-cells: small, slow, colour-sensitive, about 80% of ganglion cells. M-cells: large, fast, flicker-sensitive, about 10%.
About 90% of retinal output goes through the LGN (4 parvo layers, 2 magno, konio between) to layer 4C of V1.

outline.title: The light we see
points: Visible light is a narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum, roughly 380 to 760 nm.
Wavelength goes with hue, amplitude with intensity or brightness, and purity of wavelength with saturation.
We are sensitive to this band because there is a lot of it about and it carries information about surfaces. Colour is a subjective experience, not a property of light.

outline.title: Retinal circuitry
points: The retina is about 0.4 mm thick and wired back to front.
Receptors hyperpolarise to light with graded potentials; bipolar cells depolarise; horizontal and amacrine cells are interneurons; ganglion cells are the first to fire action potentials.
Functional chain: image formation, absorption by photopigment, electrical current in the receptor (transduction), ganglion cell activity, relay to the brain.

outline.title: Rods, cones and colour
points: Vision works across about 13 orders of magnitude of light level: scotopic (rods), mesopic (mixed), photopic (cones).
Three cone classes give thousands of colours through the pattern of activity across them; different mixes of light can look identical (metamers).
There are no blue cones in the central fovea.

outline.title: M-cells and P-cells
points: M-cells: large bodies, thick fast axons, large receptive fields, sensitive to fast flicker, not wavelength-sensitive, high contrast sensitivity, few in the fovea, about 10% of the total.
P-cells: small bodies, thin slower axons, small receptive fields, wavelength-sensitive, lower contrast sensitivity, many in the fovea, about 80%.
K-cells also exist and come back in a later lecture.

outline.title: Afterimages, the mosaic, blind spot and convergence
points: An afterimage looks bigger on a far surface than on a near one although the retinal image is unchanged: evidence for size constancy.
About 8 million cones and 120 million rods per retina; the fovea is 1.5 mm (5.2°) across with a 0.5 mm (1.7°) rod-free centre.
One million optic nerve fibres serve about 100 times as many receptors. Convergence buys sensitivity to dim light and costs spatial resolution.

outline.title: Visual pathways and the LGN
points: Primary pathway: retina, optic chiasm, optic tract, LGN, V1. Each visual hemifield projects to the opposite hemisphere. Lesser pathways go to the superior colliculus and the pulvinar.
LGN: six layers, the top four parvo and the bottom two magno, with konio cells between. Mapping is retinotopic. Only about 10% of its input is from the retina; about 60% is feedback from cortex.
V1 is also called area 17, striate cortex and calcarine cortex. The cortical map is upside down, which is no problem at all for the visual system.

decks.title: Handout 3: the retina and visual pathways
decks.summary: Prof Meese's written notes for the lecture. It adds detail the slides only hint at: the Purkinje shift, filling in at the blind spot, receptive fields, transient and sustained responses, and why the LGN is probably more than a relay.
takeaways: Purkinje shift: rods peak near 500 nm and cones near 550 nm, so greens look relatively lighter than yellows as light fades.
The blind spot is 12 to 18° from the fovea on the nasal retina; the two eyes' blind spots don't overlap, and the brain fills in even with one eye.
A receptive field is the region of retina which, when stimulated, changes that cell's response.
The visual system is 'duplex': a sensitive, low-resolution rod periphery and a high-resolution cone fovea.
Left LGN layers from top to bottom take input from R, L, R, L, L, R eyes.

outline.title: The light that we see
points: We mostly see surfaces and objects; light is the carrier.
The visible spectrum spans 380 to 760 nm.

outline.title: Anatomy and neurophysiology of the retina
points: Cones dominate the fovea and work at photopic levels; blue cones are about 10% of cones and absent from the fovea.
Interneurons respond with graded potentials and build convergence and receptive fields; ganglion cells are the first to produce action potentials.
Ganglion cells signal with a rate code: a transient burst then a sustained level, above or below the resting (spontaneous) rate.

outline.title: Transduction
points: The retinal image is a two-dimensional pattern of light that receptors turn into a neural signal.

outline.title: Visual pathways
points: About 90% of ganglion cells project to the LGN; lesser pathways go to the superior colliculus and pulvinar.
The LGN gets most of its synapses from cortex and elsewhere, which suggests it regulates the signal rather than simply relaying it.
The projection to V1 is contralateral and top-bottom transposed, with the fovea at the occipital pole.

decks.title: General fundus examination
decks.summary: The techniques for a general look at the fundus (direct, monocular indirect, modified monocular indirect and slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a condensing lens), when each is indicated, and how they compare.
takeaways: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a high-plus lens gives a stereoscopic, wide-field view; the image is real, aerial, inverted and reversed.
Lower-power Volk lens = more magnification and a narrower field (+90 D: 0.76x, wide; +78 D: 0.93x, narrower).
Indications for slit-lamp BIO include symptoms, a new patient, reduced VA, known retinal or systemic disease, cataract and high myopia.
Direct ophthalmoscopy keeps three advantages: an erect image, portability, and suitability for all patients.

outline.title: Techniques covered
points: General: direct, monocular indirect, modified monocular indirect, slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a high-plus condensing lens.
Peripheral techniques (headset BIO, contact fundus lenses, scleral indentation) follow in week 4.

outline.title: Direct ophthalmoscopy
points: Apertures and filters include wide, intermediate, macular stop, red-free, slit, fixation cross and cobalt blue.
Start with +10 D in the wheel to check the external eye and the media in at least four directions of gaze; keep both eyes open.
Disc: cup depth, rim colour, C:D ratio, ISNT rule, margins, crescents or parapapillary atrophy. Vessels: A:V ratio, nipping, tortuosity. Then mid-periphery, periphery and macula.

outline.title: Monocular indirect and modified monocular indirect
points: The Welch Allyn PanOptic gives about 5x the field of a direct ophthalmoscope; the Keeler wide-angle about 10x.
PanOptic routine: maximum aperture, centre the red dot on the filter dial, focus with the thumb lever, approach along the red reflex.
Modified monocular indirect gives a wider, moderately magnified view (4 to 5x by moving closer) but no stereopsis.

outline.title: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a condensing lens
points: Binocular and stereoscopic, with variable field and magnification and a longer working distance.
The −55 D Hruby lens gives a virtual, erect image but a tiny field (about one disc diameter) and is hard to keep in focus.

Set-up: illumination in line with the microscope, moderate parallelepiped, 10x, focus on the cornea, lens 5 to 11 mm from the eye with the 'V' pointing to the eye, then pull back until the fundus comes into focus. Use all 8 positions of gaze for the periphery.

outline.title: Indirect versus direct
points: Indirect: stereo view, larger field, view beyond the equator, works through cataract and high ametropia, longer working distance.
Direct: erect image, portable, suitable for all patients.

outline.title: Lecture MCQs
points: Field of view and magnification; magnification and Volk lens power; choosing a technique for a new 21-year-old patient. All three are in the quiz.

decks.title: Corneal topography for contact lens fitting
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_CL Corneal Topography for CL fitting_DD - no vioceover.pptx
decks.summary: What corneal shape is and how it is described (radius, eccentricity, shape factor), how keratometers and videokeratoscopes measure it, what can go wrong, and how to read axial, tangential and height maps.
takeaways: The normal cornea is a prolate ellipse: steepest at the apex, flattening to the periphery. e² = 1 − p = −Q.
Keratometry treats the tear film as a convex mirror and measures only a small central area with four points.
Keratometers use n = 1.3375 so the reading estimates total corneal power, assuming the back surface is −10% of the front.
On a map, warm colours are steep and cool colours are flat; regular astigmatism shows as a bow tie.
Axial maps are the most repeatable; tangential maps locate the apex and local detail best; height maps suit refractive surgery and simulated fluorescein.

outline.title: Corneal shape and asphericity
points: The cornea provides about two thirds of the eye's power (about 43 D). Radii range from about 7.4 to 8.8 mm, written as e.g. 7.90 @ 150; 7.85 @ 60.
Radius changes as you move from the apex; the profile is modelled as a conic section. Circle e² = 0; prolate ellipse between 0 and 1; parabola 1; hyperbola above 1; oblate ellipse below 0.
Average corneal e² is about 0.22 (e about 0.47). The two eyes are usually similar and mirror images.

outline.title: Keratometry: how it works
points: Placido (1880) and Gullstrand (1896) began it: inspect the image the cornea forms as a convex mirror.
Radius is roughly 2 × distance × image height ÷ mire separation. Correct working distance is checked with a Scheiner disc; eye movement is beaten by doubling the image with a prism.
Fixed doubling (Bausch & Lomb, one-position) or variable doubling (Javal-Schiotz, two-position).

outline.title: Assumptions, errors and uses
points: Assumes a spherical arc, principal meridians at 90°, an on-axis measure, and a back surface with −10% of the front power.
Operator errors: focusing, proximal accommodation, alignment, instrument orientation. Patient errors: distorted mires from corneal distortion, unsteady fixation.
Uses: baseline data, degree of corneal astigmatism, lens choice, RGP flexure, post-wear oedema or moulding, and verifying lens radius.

outline.title: Videokeratoscopy and map types
points: Reflection-based, covering a 7 to 9 mm area. Inaccuracies come from paraxial assumptions, tear film, fixation, focusing, bowl size, ring number and alignment.
The instrument aligns to the centre of curvature rather than the centre of the entrance pupil.
Axial (sagittal), instantaneous (tangential), height and refractive power maps each have strengths; relative and absolute colour scales are easily confused.

outline.title: Instruments, example maps and today's clinic
points: Example maps: regular, asymmetric and irregular astigmatism, keratoconus, and orthokeratology treatment.
In clinic: take three readings of each meridian for each eye and average them.

decks.title: Corneal topography: test your knowledge
decks.summary: Four multiple-choice questions on what keratometry measures, its units, the eccentricity of a hyperbola and the bow-tie pattern in against-the-rule astigmatism. The answer sheet is 'Mgmt_CLB_03_CLB Topography_test your knowledge_Ans.docx'. All four are in the quizzes for keratometry and topography.
takeaways: Keratometry gives corneal curvature, in millimetres or dioptres.
A hyperbola has e² above 1.
Against-the-rule astigmatism shows a horizontal bow tie.

decks.title: Non-traumatic red eye tutorial
decks.summary: A case-based tutorial on working out the cause of a red eye from the record: which history questions and tests matter, and comparison tables for conjunctivitis, papillae and follicles, corneal ulcers, and episcleritis, scleritis and endophthalmitis. Many slides are images of case records, so the tables are what carries over here.
takeaways: One eye: think infection, acute glaucoma or iritis. Both eyes: think conjunctivitis.
Pupil: distorted suggests iritis; oval and mid-dilated suggests angle closure.
Follicles point to viral; papillae to allergic, bacterial or contact lens causes.
Episcleritis: mild pain, normal VA, vessels move. Scleritis: moderate to severe pain, reduced VA, vessels don't move.
In the cases, watch for questions that weren't asked and tests that weren't done.

outline.title: Reading the case
points: Laterality narrows the list: unilateral for infection, acute glaucoma and iritis; bilateral for conjunctivitis.
Check what is missing from the record: questions not asked, and tests not done (for example no cover test or motility).
Pupil shape is a clue: distorted in iritis, oval and mid-dilated in acute angle closure.

outline.title: Conjunctivitis; papillae versus follicles
points: Viral: watery discharge, cold symptoms or fever, follicles; cool compresses and artificial tears.
Allergic: watery, itching, puffy lids, papillae; antihistamine drops and avoiding the allergen.
Bacterial: mucoid, crusty discharge with lids sticking; antibiotic drops or ointment.
Papillae are raised red areas with a central vessel on the palpebral conjunctiva; follicles are pale domes with vessels around them, in the lower fornix.

outline.title: Corneal ulcers
points: Infectious: contact lens wear and smoking are risks; pain, photophobia, watering, reduced VA; staining with epithelial opacity and stromal infiltrate.
Non-infectious: no lens wear, possible systemic illness (ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis); otherwise similar signs.
Marginal keratitis: no pain or photophobia, VA normal, staining with a stromal infiltrate. Recurrent corneal erosion: pain and photophobia with staining only.
Some conditions carry more than one referral urgency.

outline.title: Episcleritis, scleritis and endophthalmitis
points: Episcleritis: recent onset, mild pain, vessels move over the sclera, VA normal, clear cornea and anterior chamber.
Scleritis: moderate to severe pain, vessels do not move, VA reduced, keratic precipitates, cells and flare, possible choroiditis or retinitis.
Endophthalmitis: sudden, painful, red, with cells, flare and hypopyon.

decks.title: Multifocal lenses part 2: bifocal problems and prism control
decks.summary: The four classic bifocal problems (near centration, jump, poor acuity in the segment, aberrations), how to work out prism at the near vision point with Prentice's rule, differential prism in anisometropia, and the prism-controlled designs that fix it.
takeaways: The near vision point (NVP) is where the wearer looks; the near optical centre (ON) is where the combined prism is zero. They rarely coincide.
Prism at the NVP = distance portion prism + segment prism. Round segments give base-down at the NVP: this reduces the prism for hyperopes and adds to it for myopes.
Jump = segment-top-to-segment-centre distance (cm) × add, always base-down for round segments and independent of the distance Rx. E-style and semicircular segments have no jump.
Vertical differential prism in anisometropia comes from the distance portions; the segments cancel out if they are the same in both eyes.
Differential prism with unequal round segments = (r₂ − r₁) × add. Put the larger segment in the lens with more plus in the vertical meridian.

outline.title: Bifocal problems and the near optical centre
points: Poor near centration, image jump, poor VA in the segment (e.g. a wavy fused interface), and monochromatic and chromatic aberration.
Any point away from an optical centre has prism and more off-axis aberration.
ON is the zero-prism point of the combined distance and segment powers; it is often only theoretical.

outline.title: Prism at the near vision point
points: X = YA ÷ (F + A), where Y is the distance from the distance optical centre to the segment's optical centre and X is the distance to ON. Negative X puts ON above the distance centre.
Plus distance lenses give base-up and base-out at the NVP; minus lenses give base-down and base-in.

Example: +5.00 DS, +3.00 add, R30 segment top 10 mm down, NVP 15 mm down: 7.5Δ up − 3.0Δ down = 4.5Δ base-up. The same with −5.00 DS gives 10.5Δ base-down. A D38 with 24 mm depth puts the segment centre at the NVP, giving 7.5Δ base-down.

outline.title: Jump
points: Crossing into a round segment adds base-down prism suddenly, so objects jump and a zone is hidden until the head moves.
Jump = segment radius (cm) × add: a +3.00 add gives 3.3Δ with a 22 mm segment and 5.7Δ with a 38 mm one.
No-jump designs put the segment centre on the dividing line: E-style and semicircular (depth = radius) segments.

outline.title: Transverse chromatic aberration
points: TCA for a solid bifocal = prism at the NVP ÷ constringence (V).
High myopes with large round segments in high-index (low V) material are worst. About 0.1Δ is the average threshold for noticing it.

outline.title: Differential prism in anisometropia
points: R −1.00 DS, L −6.00 DS, 8 mm down: 0.8Δ and 4.8Δ base-down, so 4Δ base-down in the left (or base-up in the right).
With cylinders at 90 or 180, use the power in the meridian you need: a cyl at axis 180 acts fully in the vertical meridian.
For other axes Fθ = F sin²θ (not examined for prism calculations).

outline.title: Prism-controlled bifocals
points: Uses: neutralise prism at the NVP, base-in at near for exophoria or convergence insufficiency, remove differential prism, and no-jump designs.
Options: Franklin split, Presto (segment glued into a hole), extra inset (prism = (inset − convergence) × add), unequal segment sizes, and bi-prism (slab-off) lenses.
A bi-prism lens goes on the eye with least plus or most minus, and always gives base-up at near. In a focimeter the slab line shows two images of the same power.

decks.title: Multifocal worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Eight worksheets from easy to hard: working out adds, segment choice, prism at the NVP, near optical centre position, differential prism, and choosing unequal segment sizes. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_4_Multifocal worksheet answers_EH.pptx' and are worked through in the cases for the multifocals topic.
takeaways: Transpose before working out an add if the cyl forms differ.
For vertical prism, use the power in the vertical meridian (sphere plus any cyl at axis 180).
Differential prism at near comes only from the distance portions when both segments match.
Unequal-segment fixes often need segments too big to buy (47 mm, 70 mm): bi-prism or Presto lenses are the realistic alternatives.

outline.title: Worksheet 1: adds
points: Six near-minus-distance calculations, including two where one prescription must be transposed first.

outline.title: Worksheets 2 and 3: segment choice and NVP prism
points: A high myope wanting a bigger reading area: R45 versus E-style, prism at the NVP and jump.
A low hyperope with an R30: prism at the NVP and position of the near optical centre.

outline.title: Worksheets 4 and 5: horizontal and vertical differential prism
points: Work out power in each meridian, then prism from the distance portion and the segment for each eye.

outline.title: Worksheet 6: a first-time presbyope who wants bifocals
points: Compare D, round and E segments, and think about screen use with a +1.25 add.

outline.title: Worksheets 7 and 8: derivations and prism control
points: Derive X = YA ÷ (F + A) and differential prism = (r₂ − r₁) × add.
A patient with hidden anisometropia (one Rx in plus cyl, one in minus) who can't read for long in bifocals.

outline.title: Reflection and further practice
points: Questions to ask yourself about when to recommend bifocals or trifocals, and further question sets in Tunnacliffe and Janney, Fowler and Latham-Petre, and Jalie.

decks.title: Near vision assessment
decks.summary: Measuring near vision adequacy, testing accommodation in pre-presbyopes (amplitude, facility, lag), and finding a presbyope's near add: tentative add, final add and range of clear vision. Ends with two MCQs and a short-answer question; the answers are on the answer sheet.
takeaways: Near vision adequacy: read the smallest paragraph at the patient's own reading distance and record the N-number with the distance, e.g. R N6 L N6 Bin N5 @ 35 cm.
Push-up/pull-down amplitude is the average of the two end points. Binocular amplitude is 1–2 D higher than monocular. Suspect insufficiency if it is more than 1.50 D below the age norm.
Average expected amplitude (Duane-Hofstetter) = 18.5 − 0.30 × age.
Base the tentative add on age and working distance (recommended); amplitude-based (add = WD − ½ amp) is more error-prone.
Range of clear vision: far end = 1 ÷ add; near end = 1 ÷ (add + amplitude).

outline.title: Near vision adequacy
points: True near acuity (single letters) is rarely measured; instead the patient reads N-point text at their preferred distance.
Measure unaided, habitual or optimal depending on the history. Right eye first, then left, then both.
Always record the N-number with the working distance.

outline.title: Accommodative dysfunction
points: Causes: medication, idiopathic, trauma, inflammation, diabetes, Down's syndrome and cerebral palsy.
Symptoms: headache, eyestrain, near blur, difficulty reading or changing focus.
Tests: amplitude (RAF rule push-up/pull-down), facility (±2.00 flippers), lag (MEM or modified Nott dynamic retinoscopy).

outline.title: Amplitude of accommodation
points: Distance correction on; move the smallest legible print in until blur is sustained (push-up), then out until clear (pull-down); average them.
It overestimates with depth of focus and print getting bigger as it comes closer; a −3.00 lens pushes the near point out for young patients.
Duane-Hofstetter: minimum 15 − 0.25 × age, average 18.5 − 0.30 × age, maximum 25 − 0.40 × age.

outline.title: Accommodative facility and lag
points: ±2.00 DS flippers at 40 cm, counting cycles in a minute (+ and − cleared = 1 cycle).
Fail for children and adults to 30 years: under 11 cpm monocular, under 8 cpm binocular. Some suggest 7 and 5 for ages 8 to 12.
Lag is measured with dynamic retinoscopy (covered in its own lecture).

outline.title: Presbyopia and the tentative add
points: Usually starts at 40–45; earlier in hot climates, short arms and hyperopes; later in myopes. No true accommodation by about 55.
Tentative add by age and distance: e.g. at 50 years, +1.75 for 33 cm, +1.25 for 40 cm, +1.00 for 50–60 cm.
From amplitude: add = WD (D) − ½ amp. Example: 50 years, amp 3.50 D, 33 cm gives 3.00 − 1.75 = +1.25.

outline.title: Final add, range and recording
points: Binocularly, try −0.25 first; if not clearer, try +0.25; stop when clarity no longer improves. This gives the least plus.
Check the range by moving the chart in and out; if it doesn't suit, change the add or give an intermediate add.
Don't measure amplitude over 55. Adds are usually equal and rarely above +3.00 except for low vision. Unequal adds may be needed for amblyopia, lag, anisometropia or a very particular patient.

decks.title: Near vision assessment: question answers
decks.summary: Worked answers to the lecture's two MCQs and the short-answer question about CT, a 52-year-old model maker. All three are in the near vision quiz and cases.
takeaways: The tentative add should be based on age and working distance, not measured amplitude.
Average amplitude: 18.5 − 0.30 × age.
CT: +2.50 add, clear from about 18 to 40 cm, so a phone at 35 cm is fine.

decks.title: Rigid corneal lens design 1
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_Rigid Corneal lens-1 Design_DD - no vioceover.pptx
decks.summary: What rigid gas permeable lenses offer, oxygen permeability and transmissibility, the material families and how they are named, and the back-surface design of a rigid lens: edge lift and clearance, the tricurve, and aspheric designs.
takeaways: Permeability Dk is a material property; transmissibility Dk/t depends on thickness too. Dk rises with temperature, so it is quoted at 34°C.
PMMA has almost no oxygen permeability and is not counted as a rigid gas permeable material.
Fluorosilicone acrylates give medium to high Dk (40 to 100+); Menicon Z (Dk 163) was the first GP approved for 30 days' continuous wear.
USAN name, e.g. paflufocon B III 3: prefix, 'focon' = rigid, B = second formulation, III = silicone and fluorine, 3 = Dk 31–60.
Tricurve rule of thumb: BOZD = TD − 1.4; secondary curve BOZR + 1.0 mm; peripheral curve BOZR + 2.5 mm. Ideal central tear layer about 15–20 µm.

outline.title: Why rigid lenses
points: Sharper, stable vision; good oxygen; durable (a year or more); can be tailored to irregular corneas and high astigmatism; resist deposits; cost-effective over time.
Ideal material: meets oxygen needs, inert, wets well, resists spoilage, stays stable, durable, transparent and reproducible.

outline.title: Oxygen
points: Dk = diffusion coefficient × solubility; range 0 to 300 × 10⁻¹¹. Dk/t ranges 0 to 200 × 10⁻⁹; a typical GP is 0.17 mm thick.
In GPs oxygen moves mainly by diffusion through silicone; in hydrogels it is carried by water.
Equivalent oxygen percentage (EOP) compares the cornea's oxygen uptake after lens wear with calibration gas mixtures.

outline.title: Materials and classification
points: PMMA (1930s): easy to make and care for, but almost no oxygen. CAB: Dk 4–8, flexible, unstable, incompatible with BAK.
Silicone acrylates: higher Dk and larger lenses possible, but deposit-prone, scratch easily, break, craze and flex. Fluorosilicone acrylates: fewer deposits, Dk 40 to 100+, but scratch and flex.
ISO groups: suffix I no silicone or fluorine, II silicone only, III both, IV fluorine only; then a Dk band number.

outline.title: Design aims and edge lift
points: Aims: match the cornea, avoid indentation, keep tears exchanging, avoid lid irritation and decentration, minimise flare.
Forces on the lens: capillary attraction, tear meniscus, lids, friction and gravity; total diameter has the biggest effect.

Constant axial edge lift (a property of the lens) gave too much clearance on steep corneas and too little on flat ones, so designs moved to constant axial edge clearance (about 60–80 µm, or AEL 0.12–0.15 mm).

outline.title: Back surface and edge
points: A tear layer of zero means bearing and possible abrasion; you need to change BOZR by more than 0.05 mm or BOZD by more than 0.5 mm to see a fluorescein change.
A steep centre gives a tight mid-periphery; an aligned or flat centre gives moderate to flat mid-peripheral clearance.
Example tricurve: 7.80 BOZR / 8.80 secondary / 10.30 peripheral, TD 9.20 with a 7.80 BOZD, 0.4 and 0.3 mm curve widths.

outline.title: Aspheric lenses
points: Pros: better capillary attraction, less flare, no transition pressure, thinner, easier to fit, less spectacle blur.
Cons: corneal asphericity is hard to measure, centration can be poor, hard to verify, make and modify, and optics suffer if decentred.

decks.title: Rigid lens design: test your knowledge

takeaways: Prefix, 'focon' stem, formulation letter, group suffix (silicone/fluorine), Dk band number.

decks.title: Receptive fields and convolution
decks.summary: Centre-surround receptive fields of retinal ganglion cells, treated as weighting functions. Sliding a weighting function across an image (convolution) blurs it, finds edges at zero-crossings and removes redundancy, and doing it at several sizes gives neural images at several spatial scales.
takeaways: On- and off-centre cells come in equal numbers; receptive fields get bigger with eccentricity.
A cell's response is the sum of light in its excitatory region minus light in its inhibitory region; with uniform light the two cancel and it fires at its spontaneous rate.
Convolution: multiply the image by the weighting function at each position and sum. The output is a neural image.
Edges appear as zero-crossings in the neural image; uniform areas give nothing. That is data compression.
Retinal output is a set of overlapping neural images at different spatial scales, with fine scales missing in the periphery.

outline.title: Ganglion cell receptive fields (revision)
points: Mexican-hat profile: excitatory centre and inhibitory surround (on-centre), or the reverse (off-centre).
Responses: spontaneous discharge, a transient burst at onset, then a sustained (steady-state) level.
Light in an excitatory region or dark in an inhibitory region raises the response; the opposite lowers it.

outline.title: An array of cells and a luminance edge
points: Cells wholly on the light or dark side, or centred exactly on the edge, fire at the spontaneous rate.
Cells just either side of the edge fire above and below it, so the edge lies at the zero-crossing.
This is convolution, and it compresses data by removing redundancy.

outline.title: The Hermann grid
points: On-centre cells at an intersection get more surround inhibition than those on a bar, so they signal less lightness: illusory dark blobs.
Work out the off-centre case and the reversed grid for yourself.

outline.title: Convolution with Gaussians and spatial scale
points: Images and weighting functions are just numbers: multiply and sum at each location.
A wider Gaussian blurs more. Different information lives at different scales (fine hairs versus the curve of a cat's back).
Convolving with a weighting function is a form of filtering.

outline.title: Ganglion cells as filters
points: Centre-surround weighting functions at three scales blur and mark edges with zero-crossings.
Ganglion cells do three jobs: work at several scales, highlight edges, and remove redundancy.

decks.title: Handout 4: receptive fields and convolution
decks.summary: Prof Meese's notes for week 4. It explains step by step why an array of on- and off-centre cells responds to an edge as it does, defines convolution and neural images, and walks through the Hermann grid.
takeaways: The term 'receptive field' comes from Hartline (1938); Kuffler (1953) described centre-surround fields.
Ganglion cells are roughly linear: excitatory and inhibitory weights are about equal and add algebraically.
In the fovea a cell's centre may get input from a single cone; the surround always pools several receptors.
There are two complementary neural images, one for on-centre and one for off-centre cells.

decks.title: Week 4 test your knowledge: receptive fields
decks.file: VSE Week 4 Receptive fields Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Five multiple-choice questions on steady-state responses, receptive fields, the Hermann grid, the LGN and convolution. Four are in the receptive fields quiz. The answer highlighting didn't survive in the copy on Blackboard, so these answers are worked out from the lecture and handout.
takeaways: A receptive field is the region of retina that changes a cell's response.
The Hermann grid blobs come from centre-surround cells being stimulated differently at bars and intersections.
Each LGN receives the contralateral visual field.
Looking at an image through a filter is convolution.

decks.summary: The library's session on finding sources for the e-portfolio and the vision sciences assignment: building a Web of Science search, telling a primary paper from a review, finding disease information and guidance, and referencing with Cite Them Right.
takeaways: The e-portfolio is 15% of OP2521: PHE task 4.5%, AaD 3%, DoC/PaP 3%, PPD 4.5%, plus pass/fail attendance at clinic, IPL and communication sessions.

Search method: split the question into concepts, list synonyms, join synonyms with OR and concepts with AND.
Use Harvard style via Cite Them Right Online.

points: E-portfolio task weightings and why references matter.
Vision sciences: primary papers only.

outline.title: Building a search
points: Narrow the topic to one question; identify the main concepts.
Different authors use different words, so list synonyms (e.g. wellbeing, well-being, mental health, stress).
OR combines alternatives; AND combines concepts. Use filters, read abstracts, and download PDFs straight away.

outline.title: Study designs and suitable papers
points: Designs from systematic reviews and RCTs to case reports, guidelines and expert opinion.
In Web of Science, the review icon marks papers you can't use; check publication date and page count.

points: Disease information from BMJ Best Practice, NHS pages (site: search), e-books and ClinicalKey.
In guidelines and regulations, use Ctrl+F to find the key terms the question points to.

decks.title: Peripheral fundus examination
decks.summary: Head-mounted binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy, the slit-lamp contact fundus lens and scleral indentation: what each shows, when to use it and how to do it, with a short note on diagnostic drugs and a summary table of every fundus technique.
takeaways: Head-mounted BIO with a +20 D lens: stereo, about 45° field, about 3x, real inverted reversed image, and it can show the entire retina.
A contact fundus (mirror) lens gives a virtual, erect but reversed image; it needs anaesthetic and a coupling solution.
Scleral indentation is done with the patient supine, using headset BIO and a +20 D lens; the patient looks towards the indenter.
Ora serrata is about 7 mm behind the limbus; the equator 13–14 mm.
Ocular anaesthetics are highly toxic, must be refrigerated, and the dose, batch and expiry go on the record.

outline.title: Head-mounted BIO
points: Stereoscopic, wide-angle, high-resolution view; image real, magnified, laterally reversed and inverted.
Set the eyepieces to your PD, put the light in the upper half of the field, match spot size to the pupil, and hold the lens with its silver edge towards the patient.
Start with the +20 D lens close to the eye and pull it back until the red reflex fills it; keep the headset at arm's length and use all 8 gaze directions.

outline.title: Contact fundus lens
points: A specialist slit-lamp technique with a small field per mirror.
Clean the lens, anaesthetise, apply coupling fluid, pick the mirror 180° from the area of interest and rotate.

outline.title: Scleral indentation
points: Dynamic view of the far periphery. Patient supine, with headset BIO and +20 D.
Indications: far-peripheral lesions, symptoms, tobacco dust (Shafer's sign), vitreous haemorrhage, history of detachment, high myopia, or when the ora is hard to see.
Patient looks away first, place the indenter on the lid fold, then the patient looks towards it; indent without pressing on the globe.

outline.title: Diagnostic drugs (brief)
points: Mydriatics such as tropicamide 0.5–1% and phenylephrine 2.5%; check IOP before and after and the angle.
Light safety: rheostat at half power and no more than 40 seconds on one area.
Anaesthetics such as oxybuprocaine 0.4%, tetracaine 0.5%, proxymetacaine 0.5%, lidocaine 4%.

outline.title: Summary table and MCQs
points: Direct: about 15x, 5° field, to the equator. Monocular indirect: 5x, 12°. Volk lenses: stereo, beyond the equator. Headset BIO and contact lens: the whole retina.
Three MCQs on patient position and the correct statement about anaesthetics are in the quiz.

The nine protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010.

decks.title: Lagophthalmos tutorial
decks.summary: A case tutorial on a patient who can't close their eyelids fully. Most slides are images of the case record; the text covers which tests are needed, referral urgency for ectropion, and myasthenia gravis.
takeaways: Tests needed: history, VA, cover test, motility and external examination. Pupils, refraction, internal exam and IOP are not needed.
No improvement with a pinhole rules out uncorrected refractive error as the cause of reduced VA.
Ectropion: urgent (2 weeks) if the cornea stains; routine if the cornea is normal.
Myasthenia gravis: intermittent binocular diplopia varying with gaze, fatigable ptosis (worse on sustained upgaze) and lagophthalmos.

decks.title: Proptosis tutorial
decks.summary: A case tutorial on a bulging eye. It explains how carotid-cavernous fistula, orbital cellulitis and thyroid eye disease cause proptosis, and lists the features that tell them (and orbital tumour) apart.
takeaways: Carotid-cavernous fistula: arterial blood floods the cavernous sinus, orbital veins engorge, and nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI can be affected. Look for a bruit, pulsating proptosis and brick-red vessels.
Orbital cellulitis: spread from sinuses, teeth or ears; sudden unilateral proptosis, painful limited movement, possible RAPD. It can spread to the brain.
Thyroid eye disease: orbital fat and connective tissue expand; lid retraction, lagophthalmos, proptosis and incomitant deviation.
Orbital tumour: urgent (1 week) if vision, movement or the cornea are affected; routine if VA and cornea are normal.

decks.title: Progressive power lenses
decks.summary: How progressive lenses developed and how their surfaces are designed, progression laws and power along the corridor, reading iso-cylinder and mean sphere plots, short-corridor, occupational and free-form designs, the swimming effect, prism thinning, lens markings and dispensing.
takeaways: Two things decide a conventional PPL's performance: the formula for the power progression, and how the designer removes astigmatism along the meridian line (pushing it into the periphery).
Surface astigmatism rises with higher adds and shorter corridors. The corridor of clear vision is where it stays under 1.00 D.
Linear progression: add at a point = rate (D/mm) × distance below the prism checking point. Power there = distance Rx in that meridian + add.
Prism thinning is equal base-down prism in both lenses to balance edge thickness; unequal vertical prism at the prism checking point means prescribed prism.
Free-form surfaces are cut point by point, usually on the back surface, and need back vertex distance, pantoscopic tilt and wrap measurements.

outline.title: Why progressives, and how they developed
points: Bifocals and trifocals have fixed focus zones and a visible line that signals age.
Owen Aves patented the first design in 1907 but it was never made. Bernard Maitenaz's Varilux (Essel, 1959) was the first commercial success.

Varilux 1: spherical sections, large stable zones but lots of peripheral astigmatism ('hard'). Varilux 2 (1973): aspheric sections, narrower near zone but less astigmatism and easier to adapt to ('soft').

outline.title: Surface design
points: Conventional PPLs carry the progression on the front surface; the prescription is worked on the back.
A linear progression of 0.133 D/mm gives +1.33 at 10 mm and +2.00 at 15 mm. Most modern designs use non-linear laws.

Think of two spheres (distance and near radii) joined by an aspheric surface whose radius shrinks steadily. Tangential and sagittal powers must be matched along the meridian line, which pushes astigmatism to the sides.

outline.title: Plots, comparisons and short corridors
points: Iso-cylinder plots map surface astigmatism; mean sphere plots map (FT + FS) ÷ 2. Astigmatism rises with the add.
Plots are hard to compare between companies (different methods and contour steps, usually plano with +2.00 add). Many intolerances are due to poor dispensing.
Standard corridors need about 18 mm frame depth, short corridors about 14 mm but with more astigmatism. Use the right template when re-marking.

outline.title: Occupational and free-form lenses
points: Occupational lenses are prescribed from the near Rx with a degression of about −0.75 to −1.25 D towards intermediate: low rate of change, wide zones. Some aren't suitable for driving.

Free-form lenses can tailor the surface to the prescription, working distances and fitting (BVD, pantoscopic tilt, wrap), and can control prism and magnification in anisometropia. Main drawback: cost.

outline.title: Swimming and prism thinning
points: Different rates of change of astigmatism in the two lenses give different magnifications in peripheral gaze, so objects seem to move differently for each eye: the swimming feeling. Worse with higher adds and new wearers.
Base-down prism, equal in both lenses, is added by the lab to balance the thin bottom edge. Higher adds get more.

outline.title: Markings and dispensing
points: Markings: distance check circle, fitting cross, prism checking point, near check circle, plus permanent engravings (trade mark and add) 34 mm apart.
Adjust the frame first and check its depth; mark each pupil centre in the natural head position with the patient looking at your opposite eye; remove, replace and recheck.
Verify by re-marking with the manufacturer's template from the engravings.

outline.title: Alternatives
points: Lens systems, diffractive, liquid crystal, gradient index and deformable lenses.

decks.title: Progressive lens worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Three worksheets: power, prism and TCA along a linear progression; short questions on PPL design; and a dispensing scenario for a 55-year-old bank manager. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_5_PPL worksheet answers_EH.pptx' and are worked through in the PPL topic.
takeaways: Include the cyl when its axis is 180 (it acts vertically), not when it is 90.
Opposite base directions in the two eyes add to give differential prism.
Prism thinning is not a way to thin lenses: use high index or aspheric designs.

decks.title: The primary visual cortex (V1)
decks.summary: How V1 develops the retina's code: a stretched retinotopic map, orientation-selective simple, complex and end-stopped cells, why single cells can't code orientation but populations can (the tilt aftereffect), and V1's modular layout of orientation hypercolumns, ocular dominance columns and colour blobs.
takeaways: V1 is retinotopic but stretched: about half of it represents the central 10° of the visual field.
V1 is the first stage with orientation selectivity. Simple cells have separate on and off regions; complex cells care about orientation but not exact position; end-stopping is found in both.
A single cell's response is ambiguous (contrast and orientation are confounded); a hypercolumn's population response is not.
The tilt aftereffect supports population coding of orientation.
A module (about 1 mm, 100,000 cells) holds a pair of ocular dominance columns, a full set of orientations and colour blobs; there are about 2,500 modules.

outline.title: Maps
points: The retina transduces, emphasises edges, works at several scales and multiplexes contrast and colour. V1 develops this further.
2-DG autoradiography (Tootell et al., 1982) shows a retinotopic map; like a stylised Tube map, the centre gets far more space than its real size.

outline.title: Cortical receptive fields
points: Simple cells (Hubel and Wiesel): elongated on and off regions; selective for orientation, size and position. Little or no background firing.
Orientation columns: cells in a column share a preferred orientation; moving across the cortex the preference rotates, and a full set makes a hypercolumn.
Complex cells: no separate on and off regions, strongly orientation-tuned, indifferent to position. End-stopped (once 'hypercomplex') cells prefer contours that end inside the field.

outline.title: Feature detectors and their problems
points: The classic hierarchy runs from spots to oriented edges to corners to 'grandmother cells'.
Problems: an 'edge detector' also responds to bars of both polarities, there aren't enough cells for every feature, and top-down processing is ignored.
The emphasis has shifted from feature detection to population codes.

outline.title: Population codes and the tilt aftereffect
points: A medium response could be medium contrast at the preferred orientation or high contrast off it, so one cell is ambiguous.
The pattern across a hypercolumn is unambiguous.
After adapting to a tilted pattern, vertical lines look tilted the other way: adaptation shifts the population response.

outline.title: Modular organisation
points: Ocular dominance columns (LeVay et al., 1975) alternate between the eyes.
Cytochrome oxidase staining shows blobs at the centres of ocular dominance columns; blob cells are colour-selective (double-opponent).
Idealised module: two ocular dominance columns, a full set of orientations and colour blobs; about 100,000 cells, about 2,500 modules.

outline.title: Extra: a letter in the brain
points: fMRI of a W shown in the left visual field: the right hemisphere responds with an upside-down, centrally magnified pattern.

decks.title: Handout 5: the primary visual cortex
decks.summary: Prof Meese's notes on V1: research methods (single-cell recording, autoradiography, optical imaging, psychophysics), V1 anatomy and layers, cortical maps, the three classes of cortical cell and the columnar organisation for orientation, size, eye and colour.
takeaways: V1 has about 1.5 × 10⁸ neurons, about 3 × 8 cm per hemisphere and is under 2 mm thick, with six layers (layer 4 subdivided down to 4Cα and 4Cβ).
About half of V1 represents the central 10° of the visual field.
Complex cells are non-linear and prefer flicker or movement.
Blob cells: colour-selective, low spatial frequency, broadly tuned or untuned for orientation.

decks.title: Week 5 test your knowledge: visual cortex
decks.file: VSE Week 5 Visual cortex Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Fourteen multiple-choice questions on simple and complex cells, hypercolumns, ocular dominance, blobs, the modular organisation and the tilt aftereffect. Eight are in the V1 quiz. The answer highlighting didn't survive in the Blackboard copy, so the answers are worked out from the lecture and handout.
takeaways: Simple cells respond at specific retinal coordinates.
Complex cells respond to the right size and orientation anywhere in their field.
Injecting one eye gives alternating stripes in V1.
Most blob cells are not narrowly tuned for orientation.

decks.title: Clinical assessment of ocular health
decks.summary: Direct ophthalmoscopy in the routine exam: what College guidance and the Opticians Act expect, magnification and field of view, a step-by-step routine from the external eye to the macula, how to describe what you see, normal variations, and tips for small pupils and high myopes. Ends with MCQs and short-answer questions.
takeaways: Magnification is about 15x for an emmetropic fundus and 2.5x for the anterior eye through +10 D.
Field of view falls with longer working distance, smaller pupils and myopia; it rises with hyperopia.
Describe each structure; avoid 'NAD', 'WNL' and 'normal'.
A:V ratio is normally 2:3 or 1:2. CD ratio scales with disc size, so a big cup in a big disc can be normal.
In high myopia the fundus is magnified and the field small, so it's easy to miss things; consider dilating or an indirect method.

outline.title: Requirements and alternatives
points: College guidance: at minimum, direct ophthalmoscopy on the undilated eye, with other methods allowed; dilate or refer if the view isn't adequate.
The Opticians Act requires external and internal examination of the eye.
Slit lamp, photography, ultra-wide-field imaging and OCT (including OCT-A) add information.

outline.title: Magnification and field of view
points: M = (K′ ÷ 4) × 1 ÷ (1 − wK), with K′ about 60 D: about 15x for an emmetrope, more for myopes and less for hyperopes.
Useful field: j = g(K − W) ÷ K′, where g is pupil size and W the reciprocal of working distance.
Field shrinks with longer working distance, smaller pupils and myopia.

outline.title: Routine: external eye
points: Lights off, glasses off, raise the chair, give a fixation target; your right hand and right eye for their right eye.
Start at +10 D (eye in focus at 10 cm, 2.5x): red reflex, iris, pupil, cornea, lids and lashes, then the conjunctiva in each direction of gaze, reducing plus through the media.
Record descriptively, e.g. lids 'clean, full'; cornea 'clear'; iris 'brown, even colour'.

outline.title: Routine: posterior eye
points: Disc first (about 0 D if both of you are emmetropic), then the posterior pole, then 8 directions of gaze, and finally the macula with the macular stop.
Disc: CD ratio, depth, colour, margin, rim and ISNT. Distinguish the colour cup from the contour cup.
Vessels: A:V about 2:3, look for nipping (a sign of systemic disease).

outline.title: Macula, variations and tips
points: Macula: even colour, foveal reflex present (it may be absent with age-related changes).
Normal variations: tigroid (tessellated) fundus in myopes, visible choroidal vessels, crescents.
Don't rush; don't show surprise; small pupils: get close, dim the light, and let them blink. High myopes: let them keep their correction on.

decks.title: Ocular health assessment: question answers
decks.summary: Answers to the lecture's two MCQs and two short-answer questions (field of view for a +10.00 D hyperope, and the ISNT rule). All four are in the direct ophthalmoscopy and optic disc topics.
takeaways: Anterior eye magnification (2.5x) is about six times less than fundus magnification (15x).
A:V of 3:2 is not normal: arterioles are narrower.
+10.00 D, 4 mm pupil, 2.5 cm: useful field about 3.3 mm.

decks.title: Anterior chamber assessment
decks.summary: Why the anterior chamber angle matters before dilating, who is at risk of angle closure, and the ways to assess it: van Herick, pen torch, Smith's method, ultrasound, Scheimpflug imaging, AS-OCT and gonioscopy, the only one that shows the angle directly.
takeaways: Van Herick compares peripheral chamber depth to corneal thickness: grade 2 (1:¼) means dilation could cause closure.
Risk factors: shallow chamber, forward or thick lens, small cornea, short eye, steep cornea, age, female sex (4:1) and East Asian ethnicity.
Smith's method: chamber depth = slit length × about 1.4; under 2 mm suggests risk.
Gonioscopy is the gold standard and the only technique that views the angle directly.
Angle structures front to back: Schwalbe's line, unpigmented and pigmented trabecular meshwork, scleral spur, ciliary body. The superior angle is usually the narrowest.

outline.title: Why and who
points: Aqueous drains mainly through the trabecular meshwork (80–90%) and partly by the uveoscleral route.
Dilating can trigger acute angle closure: pain, blurred vision with haloes, nausea and vomiting. Warn patients before dilating.
Risk factors: shallow chamber, anterior or thick lens, small corneal diameter, short axial length, steep cornea, age, female sex, East Asian ethnicity.

outline.title: Van Herick, pen torch and Smith
points: Van Herick: 10–16x, narrow bright slit at 60° temporal at the limbus. Grade 4 ≥ 1:1, 3 = 1:½, 2 = 1:¼, 1 < 1:¼, 0 closed.
Pen torch: light parallel to the iris from the temporal side; the share of nasal iris in shadow (0, 25, 50, 75, 100%) gives grades 4 to 0. Very gross.
Smith: horizontal 1–2 mm slit at 60°, shorten it until the corneal and lens reflections meet; depth ≈ slit length × 1.4.

outline.title: Imaging
points: Ultrasound (A and B scan), Scheimpflug imaging (Pentacam, rotating blue-light slits) and AS-OCT (low-coherence interferometry with infrared).
None of these views the angle directly.

outline.title: Gonioscopy
points: Total internal reflection hides the angle; a gonio lens neutralises it.
Indications include narrow angles on van Herick (grade 2 or less), glaucoma, pigment dispersion or pseudoexfoliation, neovascular risk, trauma and after iridotomy. Not after recent trauma or surgery.
Direct (Koeppe) or indirect mirror lenses: scleral Goldmann lenses need coupling fluid; corneal 4-mirror lenses (Posner, Zeiss, Sussman) are about 9 mm.
Common errors: misreading structures, too little or too much coupling fluid, the wrong lens, and pressing too hard (which can falsely widen the angle).

outline.title: MCQs
points: Order of angle structures, and which statement is false. Both are in the quiz.

decks.title: Rigid corneal lens 2: fitting and management
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_5_Rigid Corneal lens-2 Fitting and management_DD - no vioceover.pptx
decks.summary: The rigid lens fitting routine from start to finish: choosing patients, preliminary measurements, picking a first trial lens (BOZR, total diameter, BOZD), applying and removing it, grading dynamic and static fit, and adjusting power when the BOZR changes.
takeaways: Good candidates: motivated, moderate to high Rx, stable corneal toricity, residual cylinder under 0.75 D.
BOZR by corneal astigmatism: under 0.50 DC, 0.05 mm steeper than flat K; 0.50–1.00 DC, 0.05–0.10 mm steeper; 1.00–2.00 DC, a third of the difference steeper; over 2.00 DC, toric.
Total diameter about 2 mm smaller than HVID (usually 8.50–10.50 mm). BOZD about 1 mm larger than the pupil in average light.
Sagittal depth decides the fit: steeper BOZR or bigger diameter = steeper fit.
For every 0.05 mm the BOZR steepens, the tear lens adds +0.25 D, so make the lens power 0.25 D more minus (and vice versa).

outline.title: Patient selection and measurements
points: Motivation, moderate to high Rx, astigmatism (better vision than soft toric), myopia control.
Against-the-rule toricity tends to cause decentration and residual astigmatism with spherical GPs.
Measure keratometry, HVID, lid positions and tension, pupil size in bright and dim light, an accurate spectacle Rx, and ocular health. Plus and high-power lenses are made larger.

outline.title: Choosing the first trial lens
points: Trial sets need low and high minus and plus, suitable diameters and BOZRs.
BOZR from flat K and corneal toricity (rule above); a smaller BOZD for steeper corneas.
Thickness affects comfort and oxygen; the edge profile affects comfort, stability, wear time, tear flow and removal.

outline.title: Application, settling and power
points: Warn the patient about lid sensation in calm words; eyes shut briefly, then look down while blinking.
Let the lens settle (10–20 minutes) so tears don't wash out the fluorescein or exaggerate movement.

Power: e.g. trial 8.00 / −2.00, over-refraction −1.50 → −3.50; ordering 8.10 instead makes the tear lens 0.50 D more minus, so order −3.00. Ignore cylinders under 1.00 D; check with a +1.00 blur test. Empirical fitting succeeds 40–85% of the time.

outline.title: Dynamic fit
points: Sagittal height (BOZR with diameter) controls the fit.
Grade comfort (0–10), coverage (−2 to +2 against HVID), centration (crossing limbus or pupil, or contained) and movement between blinks (−2 for under 0.5 mm to +2 for over 2 mm).

outline.title: Static fit with fluorescein
points: Use a little fluorescein with cobalt blue and a yellow (Wratten 12) filter; grade central, mid-peripheral and edge zones in each principal meridian.
Ideal: alignment centrally (about 20 µm tear layer), mid-peripheral alignment and an even edge band; most lenses land in a three-point-touch pattern.
Pooling means the lens is steeper than the cornea there; dark areas mean touch.

decks.title: Rigid lens fitting: test your knowledge
decks.summary: A fluorescein-pattern short-answer question and four MCQs on siloxane acrylates, the benefits of rigid lenses, tear layer thickness and peripheral curves. The highlighting on the answer sheet ('Mgmt_CLB_04_CLB RCL-fitting_test your knowledge_Ans.docx') didn't survive, so the answers in the quiz are worked out from the lectures; the peripheral-curve question is left out because its answer can't be confirmed from the slides.
takeaways: Ideal central tear layer: 15–20 µm.
Rigid lenses carry a lower infection risk than soft lenses.
A spherical lens fitted on flat K on a with-the-rule cornea gives a horizontal band of alignment with pooling above and below.

decks.title: Effective applications (careers talk)
decks.summary: Aston Careers on building a professional identity, writing a tailored CV and cover letter, answering competency-based questions with STAR, and interview tips. Book help through Aston Futures; CV360 gives instant CV feedback.
takeaways: Tailor your CV to each role and avoid templates; give evidence of skills in context.
Competency questions ('Tell us about a time when…') assume past behaviour predicts future performance; examples don't have to come from optometry.
Structure answers with STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

decks.title: Aberrations of spectacle lenses
decks.summary: What a perfect image is, why first-order (paraxial) optics predicts one and third-order optics doesn't, the five Seidel aberrations and which matter for spectacle lenses, how to calculate oblique astigmatic error, mean oblique power and error, and longitudinal and transverse chromatic aberration.
takeaways: First-order optics uses sin i ≈ i (accurate to about 5°) and always predicts a perfect image. Third-order adds the i³/3! term (good to about 20°) and gives the five Seidel aberrations.
Spherical aberration and coma are ignored in spectacle design: the pupil limits them and the eye's own aberrations swamp them.
Oblique astigmatism matters most; best-form or aspheric lenses control it.
OAE = FT − FS; MOP = (FT + FS) ÷ 2; MOE = MOP − F′v, with FT and FS measured from the vertex sphere.
TCA = prism ÷ V (= F × c ÷ V); about 0.1Δ is noticeable. LCA = F ÷ V and is masked by the eye's own.

outline.title: Perfect images, first- and third-order optics
points: A perfect image: every object point imaged as a point, arranged in a geometrically similar way.
sin i = i − i³/3! + i⁵/5! − …. First-order (paraxial, Gaussian) uses the first term; Snell's law becomes ni = n′i′.
Third-order (Seidel) uses two terms and shows that rays no longer meet at one point.

outline.title: Spherical aberration and coma
points: A lens is a series of prisms; if prism rises too fast towards the edge, marginal rays focus closer than paraxial ones (positive SA).
Coma compares where oblique marginal rays meet with the principal ray; it grows with ray height and angle.
Neither is considered in lens design.

outline.title: Oblique astigmatism and curvature of field
points: An oblique narrow pencil forms tangential and sagittal line foci with a disc of least confusion between.
Measure from the vertex sphere (centred on the eye's centre of rotation); the ideal image lies on the far point sphere, one back vertex focal length away.
Removing oblique astigmatism leaves a single curved image shell: curvature of field, which can partly match the far point sphere.

outline.title: Worked example
points: +500 mm lens, 25 mm from the centre of rotation, 40° off axis: fT′ = 494 mm, fS′ = 502 mm.

outline.title: Distortion
points: Barrel: points pulled towards the axis (magnification falls off-axis, minus lenses). Pincushion: pushed outwards (plus lenses).
The brain adapts, but changing lens form in a high prescription can cause complaints; some myopes prefer flat lenses despite more distortion.

outline.title: Chromatic aberration
points: Refractive index varies with wavelength (quoted at the helium d line, 587.56 nm). V (Abbe number) is the reciprocal of dispersive power.
LCA = F ÷ V, masked by the eye's own.
TCA = P ÷ V gives colour fringes in the periphery of high-power, high-index lenses. +6.00 at 12 mm: 0.12Δ in CR39 (V 60), 0.18Δ in V 40 material.

outline.title: Wavefront aberration
points: Aberrations can also be described as the optical path difference (in µm) between the real wavefront and a perfect reference sphere.

decks.title: Aberration worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Four worksheets: short explanations of first- and third-order optics and the aberrations; OAE, MOP and MOE calculations; TCA in a high-index lens; and a myope unhappy with new spectacles. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_6_Aberrations worksheet answers_EH.pptx' and are worked through in the aberrations topic.
takeaways: Subtract the lens-to-vertex-sphere distance from the focal distances before converting to powers.
TCA can be worked out as prism × dispersive power, since dispersive power = 1 ÷ V.
A change of lens form can explain 'something's not right' even when VA, Rx and centration are all fine.

decks.title: The ventral stream
decks.summary: Beyond V1: over 30 richly connected visual areas, the evidence for separate 'what' (temporal) and 'where' (parietal) streams, and the ventral stream from V2 (illusory contours, cytochrome oxidase stripes) through V4 (colour and curvature) to IT (complex shapes and faces), with the clinical conditions that follow damage.
