takeaways: Moving up the hierarchy, receptive fields grow, maps get cruder and selectivity becomes more complex. There is feedback everywhere.
Retrograde tracers (Baizer et al., 1991) show parietal and temporal streams draw on separate cells in V1, V2, V4 and MT.
V2 cells respond to illusory contours such as the Kanizsa triangle; V1 cells don't.
V4: colour (damage gives achromatopsia), some colour constancy, and selectivity for curves.
IT: 'elaborate' cells for complex pattern combinations and face cells; individual faces are probably coded by populations of about 100 cells, not grandmother cells.

outline.title: The visual hierarchy
points: Over 30 areas and over 300 connections (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991); mainly feed-forward but with feedback and lateral links.
Areas to know: V1, V2, V3, V4, MT (V5), MST, 7a, PO (V6), IT.

outline.title: Two streams
points: Anterograde and retrograde tracers map connections; Baizer et al. found the parietal and temporal streams segregated.
Parietal damage: optic ataxia, ocular apraxia and simultanagnosia (together, Balint's syndrome). Temporal damage: visual agnosia.

outline.title: V2
points: Cytochrome oxidase shows thick stripes (stereo), thin stripes (colour, from V1 blobs) and interstripes (form, from V1 interblobs).
Peterhans and von der Heydt (1991): V2 cells respond to illusory contours, which helps break camouflage.

outline.title: V4
points: Crude retinal map, columns for colour, some colour constancy.
Achromatopsia (V4 damage) versus loss of form with preserved colour (e.g. carbon monoxide damage to V1/V2 interblobs and interstripes).
Some V4 cells prefer particular curves and complex patterns (single-cell and fMRI evidence).

outline.title: IT and face recognition
points: Columns of 'elaborate' cells for combinations of features (Tanaka, 1993).
Prosopagnosia seems to show a face area, but fair tests need within-class discrimination (a farmer's cows, a birdwatcher's birds).
Face cells in IT respond to many faces (Rolls and Tovee, 1995); a face is coded by the population.

outline.title: V3 and summary
points: V3: large fields, strongly orientation-selective, input from the transient magno pathway, some wavelength selectivity shown with isoluminant stimuli; perhaps 'dynamic form'.

decks.title: Handout 6: beyond V1 (ventral and dorsal streams, part 1)
decks.summary: Prof Meese's notes covering weeks 6 and 8: the visual hierarchy, V1 revision, cortical blindness and blindsight, V2 and illusory contours, the two-streams model and the ventral pathway through V4 to IT.
takeaways: V1 damage causes cortical blindness, though the retina and LGN are intact; blindsight shows some information reaches cortex by other routes.
The two-streams idea comes from Ungerleider and Mishkin (1982).
V4 colour regions are called globs; V4 is now known to handle curvature and intermediate-complexity form too.

decks.title: Week 6 test your knowledge: the ventral stream
decks.file: VSE Week 6 Ventral stream Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Seven multiple-choice questions on prosopagnosia, blindsight, the visual hierarchy, cortical organisation and V2 illusory contours. Six are in the ventral stream quiz; the answers are worked out from the lecture and handout.
takeaways: Not recognising family faces is prosopagnosia.
Responding to unseen objects is blindsight.
You can't predict higher-level responses from responses to spots of light.
Many V2 cells respond to illusory contours.

decks.title: Clinical assessment of pupil function
decks.summary: Normal pupils and their nerve supply, how to test size, light and near responses and RAPD, how to record findings, and the main afferent and efferent anomalies: RAPD, Adie's pupil, third nerve palsy, Argyll Robertson pupil and Horner's syndrome.
takeaways: Afferent defects cause an RAPD but not anisocoria; efferent defects cause anisocoria but not an RAPD.
Nothing affects the near response without also affecting the light response. Cataract and refractive error never cause an RAPD.
Anisocoria worse in bright light means a parasympathetic problem (larger pupil abnormal); worse in the dark means sympathetic, e.g. Horner's (smaller pupil abnormal).
A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil needs immediate referral (possible posterior communicating artery aneurysm).
About 20% of people have physiological anisocoria: small, long-standing and the same in bright and dim light.

outline.title: Normal pupils and pathways
points: Equal, round, constrict to light and near; dilation is slower than constriction. 2–4 mm in bright light, 4–8 mm in dim; smaller with age; not affected by sex, iris colour or refractive error.
Parasympathetic (4 neurons): retina to pretectal nucleus, to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, via III to the ciliary ganglion, then short ciliary nerves to the sphincter.
Sympathetic (3 neurons): hypothalamus to ciliospinal centre, to superior cervical ganglion, then along the carotid with V1 and long ciliary nerves to the dilator.

outline.title: Testing and recording
points: Observe size, shape and centration (+2 D at 50 cm with the ophthalmoscope); direct and consensual responses with a distant target, light from below at 5–10 cm.
Near response: light-near dissociation occurs in Adie's, Parinaud's and Argyll Robertson pupils.
Swinging flashlight: 2–3 seconds per eye, swapping within a second; the eye with an RAPD dilates. Record e.g. 'PERRLA D+C, no RAPD, 4 mm R and L', or 'RAPD +ve LE 0.4 log'.

outline.title: Afferent defects
points: Retina, optic nerve, chiasm, tract or pretectal area; no anisocoria; near reflex normal.

A clinically detectable RAPD implies a unilateral partial optic nerve lesion (optic neuritis, AION, compression) or extensive retinal disease (detachment, CRVO, advanced glaucoma). Symmetrical damage gives no RAPD.
Absolute pupillary defect: the blind eye has no direct response and gives no consensual response in the other eye.

outline.title: Efferent defects and anisocoria
points: Anisocoria without RAPD.
Physiological: difference usually under 1 mm, the same in light and dark, long-standing, normal reflexes.
Small pupils: infants, elderly, long-standing diabetes, iritis, cholinergic drugs. Large pupils: anxiety, anticholinergics, afferent lesions.

outline.title: Specific anomalies
points: Adie's tonic pupil: post-ganglionic parasympathetic damage, young women, slow re-dilation, vermiform movements, light-near dissociation; 0.1% pilocarpine constricts it.
Third nerve palsy with the pupil involved: ptosis, down-and-out eye, dilated unreactive pupil that pilocarpine 0.1% won't constrict; commonly a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Argyll Robertson (neurosyphilis): small irregular pupils with light-near dissociation. Horner's: mild ptosis, raised lower lid, miosis, dilation lag, reduced sweating; cocaine 4% fails to dilate the pupil.

outline.title: Shape anomalies, iritis and MCQs
points: Corectopia, coloboma (inferior), polycoria, ischaemic or surgical damage. Acute changes in pupil shape need immediate referral.
Iritis: small pupil and posterior synechiae.
Three MCQs on the rules of thumb, anisocoria and Horner's are in the quiz.

decks.title: Routine eye examination
decks.summary: The order of a routine eye examination and how to fill in each section of the Aston record card: introducing yourself, history and symptoms, unaided and aided vision, focimetry, cover test, motility and pupils, anterior and posterior eye, refraction, binocular vision checks, near vision and advice. Ends with test-your-knowledge questions on pupils.
takeaways: Introduce yourself as a student optometrist working under supervision, and confirm identity and how the patient wants to be addressed.
Record negative findings in the history (e.g. headaches 0, diplopia 0, flashes 0, floaters 0).
Always do the swinging flashlight test: an RAPD is only found by comparing the two eyes.
Only test the near pupil reflex if the light reflex is abnormal.
Address the reason for visit in your advice.

outline.title: Structure and introductions
points: The flow chart assumes tonometry, fields and imaging are pre-screening; you'll have 50 minutes in stage 2 assessments and year 3 clinics.
GOC standard 2.2 and the 2025 Standards for Students: identify yourself and that you work under supervision.
Complete every general information field on the card.

outline.title: History, vision and focimetry
points: Reason for visit in the patient's words; record negative findings.
Measure unaided vision if no Rx is worn, it is lost or not always worn (drivers), or for a report.
Focimetry: age of Rx, lens type, powers, CD and add, then VA with each pair. Cover test aided, and unaided if accommodation is suspected.

outline.title: Motility and pupils
points: Motility without Rx at about 40 cm.
Pupil size in light and dark, direct and consensual reflexes, swinging flashlight test; grade abnormal responses 0 to 4+.

Horner's (anisocoria worse in the dark, ptosis, normal reflexes; refer) versus Adie's (worse in light, poor light reflex, better near response; usually no referral). Use a dim secondary light for dark irides.

outline.title: Anterior and posterior eye
points: Slit lamp preferred for detail; draw anything abnormal.
Record each structure descriptively, e.g. CD 0.3, disc orange/pink, margins well defined, ISNT, A:V 2:3, foveal reflex present.

outline.title: Refraction, binocular vision, near and advice
points: Measure PD, set up the trial frame; a PD different from the old CD may mean prism.
Monocular subjective for strong dominance; binocular for hyperopes, pseudomyopes, antimetropes, latent nystagmus and cyclophoria.

Post-refraction cover test (always for a first or much-changed Rx), Maddox rod and wing, Mallett unit, NPC and jump convergence; near add from the tentative table. Always address the reason for visit.

outline.title: Test your knowledge
points: An Adie's pupil MCQ and two short-answer questions on RAPD and physiological anisocoria; answers are in the pupils topic.

decks.title: Routine eye examination: test-your-knowledge answers
decks.file: AaM_6_Routine Eye Examination TYK Qs with answers.docx
decks.summary: Worked answers to the Adie's pupil MCQ and the RAPD and physiological anisocoria short-answer questions. All three are in the pupils topic.
takeaways: Adie's: about 2 per 1,000, parasympathetic damage at the ciliary ganglion, women aged 20 to 40, usually idiopathic.
RAPD is tested with the swinging flashlight test.
Physiological anisocoria: under 1 mm, equal in bright and dim light, normal reflexes.

decks.title: PHE introduction and infection control in optometric practice
decks.file: Prof_PHE_6_Introduction and Infection Control in Optometric Practice_AS and SR.pptx
decks.summary: How the stage 2 PHE theme runs and is assessed, then Dr Steve Russell on infection control: the law, the chain of infection, hand hygiene, gloves, decontaminating equipment and trial contact lenses, prions, storing drugs, clinical waste and universal precautions. Ends with practice MCQs for the pass/fail quiz.
takeaways: The infection control Blackboard quiz is 10 questions, open book, pass mark 50%, due Friday of week 11 at 1 pm; you must pass it to pass stage 2.
Handwashing is the single most effective way to break the chain of infection: at least 15–20 seconds using the six-stage technique.
Alcohol rubs need at least 70% alcohol to work against MRSA; they don't work on visibly dirty hands, C. difficile or norovirus.
Trial lenses and reusable tonometer heads: clean, soak in 10,000 ppm sodium hypochlorite, rinse, then disinfect as usual. Alcohol wipes alone don't remove prions.
Use universal precautions: if you'd need to change your routine for a known infectious patient, your routine isn't good enough.

outline.title: The PHE theme in stage 2
points: Sessions: infection control, practitioner health and wellbeing (week 8), public health initiatives and guidance (week 19).
Assessment: the infection control quiz, a portfolio task on wellbeing (sign-off for GOC outcome 5.6), and the summer exams.

outline.title: Why infection control and the law
points: GOC outcomes 5.5 (infection prevention) and 4.8 (health and safety), finally signed off in stage 4 CLiP.
The GOS contract requires infection control and decontamination; the 1999 health and safety regulations make the employer responsible for risk assessment; the Opticians Act sets a duty of care.

outline.title: Microbes and the chain of infection
points: Bacteria (Staph aureus, MRSA, C. difficile), fungi, protozoa (Acanthamoeba), viruses (adenovirus, norovirus).
Break the chain at any link: reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission (mostly hands), portal of entry, susceptible host.
Airborne (a sneeze has about 20 times the 100,000 particles of a cough) or contact, direct or via equipment. Catch it, bin it, kill it.

outline.title: Hand hygiene
points: NICE: wash before and between patients, around contact lenses, eye contact and drops, after soiled materials, and before and after gloves.
Remove jewellery, cover cuts, keep nails short; liquid soap in disposable containers; 4% chlorhexidine for outbreaks and invasive procedures; paper towels, no reusable towels.
Alcohol rub before lens insertion has negligible effect on comfort or wettability if left to dry. Gloves for invasive procedures, cracked hands or infective patients; wash hands anyway.

outline.title: Equipment and trial lenses
points: Contact points: charts, Amsler grids, field buttons, tonometer prisms, chin and head rests, chairs.
Cleaning removes visible dirt, disinfection reduces microbes, sterilisation destroys them all. Alcohol damages Volk lens cement; acetone, alcohol and peroxide damage gonio lenses.
Reused trial lenses: don't let them dry, clean, 10,000 ppm hypochlorite for an hour, rinse, then routine disinfection. Keep records and tell patients the risks.
The 2009 prion guidance prefers single-use items; otherwise rinse, detergent, rinse, 1% hypochlorite for 10 minutes, three rinses.

outline.title: Solutions, drugs, waste and high-risk patients
points: Date multidose bottles when opened; don't touch the tip; single-use drugs are preferred.
Drug fridge at 2–8°C with no food, checked daily, lockable, with records kept at least a year.
Clinical waste under the Controlled Waste Regulations 1992. Treat everyone as potentially infectious (universal precautions), including for COVID-19.

outline.title: Sample MCQs
points: Two practice questions on alcohol rubs and handwashing; both are in the quiz.

decks.title: Recording and grading the anterior eye
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_6_Recording and Grading Anterior Eye_DD - No vioceover.pptx
decks.summary: Why we grade the anterior eye, the main grading scales and how photographic and painted scales differ, why to grade in 0.1 steps, and how to choose and use a camera for anterior eye imaging, including resolution, compression and objective grading.
takeaways: Grading helps monitor change, tell normal from abnormal, and let another clinician continue care.
Five-point scale: 0 normal, 1 trace (rarely needs action), 2 mild (possibly), 3 moderate (usually), 4 severe (action required).
Grade to 0.1: a one-unit step is clinically significant, and whole numbers hide real change. Inter-observer variation can be up to 55%.
Photographic scales (e.g. CCLRU) are realistic but need a huge image library; painted scales (e.g. Efron) can show severity systematically but look less real.
Always say which scale you used.

outline.title: Why grade
points: Monitor disease, separate physiological from pathological, and hand over care.
A 5-point scale suits most of routine practice (7-point is more sensitive); add + or − for detail and extrapolate to conditions not on the card.

outline.title: Scales
points: Painted and photographic scales from several sources (Efron, CCLRU, Annunziato, Andersen and others).
Photographic: a huge library is needed, it's hard to match magnification and angle, and patients differ. Painted: less realistic but severity steps are systematic.
Morphing image sequences didn't improve grading over verbal or photographic scales.

outline.title: Grading in practice
points: Grading clusters on round numbers; 50 optometrists grading one image gave 1.2 ± 0.5.
Grade to 0.1: e.g. 2.5 to 3.4 is a real change hidden by rounding both to 3.
Grade bulbar and limbal redness, palpebral redness and roughness, and staining (CCLRU staining by area: under 15% to over 45%).

outline.title: Digital imaging
points: A picture replaces lengthy descriptions and can be measured.

Consider camera, slit-lamp optics, illumination, storage and support. CCD versus CMOS sensors; one-chip (mosaic, interpolated) versus three-chip (full colour fidelity, but expensive and needs more light).

outline.title: Resolution, compression and objective grading
points: The smallest features (microcysts and punctate staining, about 30 µm) need a 2 × 2 pixel matrix.
Edge detection and colour extraction (red ratio for hyperaemia, green for staining) allow objective grading, e.g. Keratograph 5M redness scans.

outline.title: Today's clinic
points: Grade two patients for redness and roughness (0.5 steps) and staining (0.1 steps), and name the scale.

decks.title: Recording and grading: test your knowledge
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_04_CLB Recording and grading_test your knowledge_Q.docx
decks.summary: A short-answer question on the benefits of grading scales and two MCQs on scale types. The answer sheet is 'Mgmt_CLB_04_CLB recording and grading_test your knowledge_Ans.docx'; all three are in the grading topic.
takeaways: Benefits: better record keeping, standardisation, monitoring and patient communication.
CCLRU is photographic.
Painted scales lack realism.

decks.title: Diplopia tutorial
decks.summary: A case tutorial on double vision. Most slides are case-record images; the text gives the cranial nerve supply of the eye muscles and a profile for each cause: internuclear ophthalmoplegia, gaze palsy, decompensated phoria, and sixth, fourth and third nerve palsies.
takeaways: SO4 LR6 (rest)3: superior oblique by IV, lateral rectus by VI, the rest by III.
Sixth nerve palsy: horizontal diplopia, esotropia, limited abduction.
Fourth nerve palsy: vertical or oblique diplopia, hypertropia, head tilted to the opposite shoulder.
Third nerve palsy: oblique diplopia, exotropia and hypotropia, limited adduction, elevation and depression, and possible pupil involvement.
In the cases, palsies come with swollen discs (papilloedema) and need careful decisions about safe dilation; INO suggests multiple sclerosis.

decks.title: Lens design: best-form lenses and Tscherning's ellipses
decks.summary: Which aberrations spectacle lens designers try to control, what a best-form lens is, the three design philosophies (point focal, Percival and minimum tangential error), reading field diagrams, Tscherning's ellipses, and how lens form and material affect dispensing decisions.
takeaways: Designers care about oblique astigmatism, curvature of field, TCA and distortion. Lens form changes nothing on-axis.
Best form: surface curves chosen to eliminate or minimise a stated defect for a set object distance, centre of rotation distance and refractive index.
Point focal: zero OAE. Percival: zero MOE (MOP = BVP). Minimum tangential error: tangential power = BVP; most modern designs.
Tscherning's ellipses give two solutions (flatter Ostwalt, steeper Wollaston) for powers from about −22 D to +7 D; outside that range you need aspheric surfaces.
High myopes often prefer flatter lenses. Only use higher index if it really makes the lens thinner, because TCA rises.

outline.title: What designers control
points: With only two spherical surfaces you can eliminate one aberration and reduce another; the best design for one patient isn't for another.
TCA: choose high-V material. Distortion: the brain adapts unless the Rx or form changes a lot. Oblique astigmatism and curvature of field: change the lens form.
Curved form: one surface convex and the other concave in all meridians (BS EN ISO 13666).

outline.title: Field diagrams and design philosophies
points: Plot tangential and sagittal vertex sphere powers against eye rotation: OAE = T − S, MOP = (T + S) ÷ 2, MOE = MOP − BVP.
+4.00 D examples: flat form has high OAE and MOE; shallow meniscus gives zero MOE (Percival); steeper gives zero tangential error (also least chromatic); steep gives zero OAE (point focal).
Minimum T-error behaves like point focal if the vertex distance increases and like Percival if it decreases.

outline.title: Tscherning's ellipses
points: Tscherning used third-order optics to find the forms free from oblique astigmatism; the relationships plot as ellipses.
For +5.00 D: +12.50/−7.50 (Ostwalt, flatter, used in practice) or +19.00/−14.00 (Wollaston).
Each plot assumes a design aim, object distance, refractive index, centre of rotation distance and thin lenses. No solution above about +7 D or below about −22 D.

outline.title: Dispensing considerations
points: −4.00 D: the best form gives slightly positive MOE (too little minus at the edges, which a young patient can't accommodate away); plano-concave gives larger negative MOE, which a non-presbyope can accommodate for, but distortion rises faster.
High myopes may prefer flat forms; changing a patient's form can cause adaptation problems.
Higher index means lower V and more TCA, so only use it if it's significantly thinner for that frame. Generally dispense best-form curved designs.

decks.title: Lens design worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Five worksheets: OAE, MOP and MOE from given powers, focal lengths and a field diagram; using Tscherning's ellipses; and keeping a high-plus prescription thin on a budget. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_8_lens design worksheet answers_EH.pptx' and are worked through in the aberrations topic.
takeaways: In a Percival lens MOP equals the BVP; in a zero tangential error lens the tangential power equals the BVP.
Use F1 = F′v − F2 (thin lens) to get the front curve from Tscherning's back curve.
Frame choice (small, round, plastic, CD = PD) is the cheapest way to make plus lenses thinner.

decks.title: The dorsal stream
decks.summary: The dorsal ('where', or 'action') stream: blindsight, MT and its direction columns and pattern cells, akinetopsia, MST and optic flow, coordinate frames in 7a and PO, Zeki's four-pathway model, and Milner and Goodale's perception/action split.
takeaways: MT (V5) has large receptive fields and columns for direction of motion; it handles relative motion, depth from motion and disparity, and grouping.
V1 codes the components of a plaid; MT 'pattern cells' code the overall motion we actually see.
Damage to MT on both sides causes akinetopsia (motion blindness).
MST cells (fields of 30–50°) prefer complex motion such as expansion, rotation and spirals, which suits optic flow during self-motion.
Milner and Goodale: the ventral stream serves perception and the dorsal stream serves action. Patient DF couldn't report a slot's orientation but could post a card through it.

outline.title: Streams and blindsight
points: Dorsal route: V1 to V2 to MT to MST to area 7a in parietal cortex.
A lesser route (retina, superior colliculus, pulvinar, parietal cortex) bypasses V1, which may explain blindsight: V1 is needed for conscious vision but isn't where seeing happens.

outline.title: MT (V5)
points: Receptive fields of 5–10° (V1 about 0.5°); columns for direction, with opposite directions across one axis.
Cells respond to planar and relative motion; motion boundaries help separate objects.
For two crossed drifting gratings, V1's population codes the two components, but MT pattern cells code the single upward motion we see.

outline.title: Akinetopsia, MST and optic flow
points: Bilateral MT damage: the world looks like snapshots, so pouring tea or crossing the road is hard.
MST: very large fields, tuned to expansion, contraction, rotation and spirals; perception follows the global pattern rather than local dots.
These patterns arise naturally as we move through the world (optic flow).

outline.title: Coordinate frames
points: Retinocentric (position on the retina), egocentric (relative to me), allocentric (relative to other objects).
Area 7a combines vision with head and body position; gaze-locked cells only respond when the animal looks in the right direction.
PO 'real position' cells have receptive fields that aren't fixed on the retina, perhaps building an allocentric map.

outline.title: More than two streams?
points: Zeki: cross-talk (e.g. V4 to MT) and four pathways: motion, colour, form with colour, and form without colour. V3 doesn't fit the what/where scheme well.

Milner and Goodale relabelled the streams perception (ventral) and action (dorsal). DF (ventral damage, visual form agnosia) could post but not report orientation; optic ataxia (dorsal damage) shows the reverse.
Evidence from illusions in healthy people is still debated.

decks.title: Handout 8: beyond V1 (part 2)
decks.summary: Prof Meese's notes on Zeki's four parallel streams and Milner and Goodale's action/perception model, including the Titchener (Ebbinghaus) circles experiments on whether grasping is fooled by illusions, and the arguments over them.
takeaways: Zeki's pathways: form without colour (M cells to V1 4B to V3), form with colour (P cells, interblobs, interstripes, V4), colour (P cells, blobs, thin stripes, V4), motion (M cells, V1 4B, thick stripes, MT).
Aglioti et al. (1995) found grip size wasn't fooled by the Titchener circles illusion; Franz et al. (2000) couldn't replicate this.
The split is now sometimes called 'what' versus 'how'.

decks.title: Week 8 test your knowledge: the dorsal stream
decks.file: VSE Week 8 Dorsal stream Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Twelve multiple-choice questions on area names, the specialisation of areas, real position cells, cytochrome oxidase, the two-streams models, patient DF and population coding. Eight are in the dorsal stream quiz; answers are worked out from the lectures and handouts.
takeaways: V1 = area 17.
Real position cells have fields that move on the retina.
Milner and Goodale: action/perception.
Four cells with five response levels each can code 5⁴ = 625 faces.

decks.title: History and symptoms (narrated lecture)
decks.file: Mgmt_AaM_8_History and Sxs narrated lecture slides_AS.pptx
decks.summary: How to take a full history and symptoms: record abbreviations, communication, general observations, the reason for visit followed up with LOFTSEA, the standard symptom check, ocular history, general health, medication, allergies, family history, and occupation, hobbies and driving, with a recorded example. (The same slides were posted as the pre-recorded lecture.)
takeaways: LOFTSEA: Location, Onset, Frequency, Type and severity, Self-treatment, Effect on the patient, Associated symptoms.
Ask every patient about distance and near vision, eyestrain, headaches, pain or burning, diplopia, and flashes and floaters.
Record negative answers: legally, no record means the question wasn't asked.
Diplopia that goes when one eye is closed is binocular; if it doesn't, it's monocular (cataract, irregular astigmatism).
Smoking is the strongest environmental risk factor for AMD; be ready to explain why you ask.

outline.title: Records and communication
points: Electronic records (Xeyex in the Aston clinic) are legible, linkable and easy to refer from, but you can't sketch and systems differ.
Know the common abbreviations (RFV, LEE, LME, OH, FOH, b.d., t.d.s., p.r.n., 2/52 and so on).
Ask permission to take a history; show empathy, active listening and open body language; don't interrupt.

outline.title: General observation, RFV and LOFTSEA
points: Notice appearance, head posture, facial asymmetry, lids and eyes, speech and emotional state.
Open with 'Is there any particular reason for your visit today?'
Follow up with LOFTSEA; sudden onset can mean serious pathology, and problems are more likely minor if the patient has done nothing about them.

outline.title: Symptom check
points: Constant distance blur: myopia, or nuclear sclerosis in older people. Intermittent: diabetes, pseudomyopia. Near blur in good light only: presbyopia. Both: astigmatism or pathology.
Visual headaches are usually mild, dull, above or behind the eyes and linked to eye use; only a minority of headaches are visual.
Pain or burning often means dry eye. Ask if double vision clears with one eye closed and whether it's vertical or side by side. Flashes suggest PVD, with detachment risk higher in high myopes.

outline.title: Ocular history
points: Spectacles (each pair: type, use, age, source, satisfaction), contact lenses (type, hours, days, care, last aftercare), low vision aids, previous injuries, infections, surgery, patching, and last eye exam.

outline.title: Health, family and lifestyle
points: Ask specifically about high blood pressure and diabetes; for each, how long and when last checked.
Medication (including drops, hay fever and contraceptive pills) and allergies or reactions to drops; check the BNF.
Family: strabismus, glaucoma, hypertension and diabetes risks rise with affected relatives. Occupation, sport, hobbies, driving and smoking.

outline.title: Tips and recording
points: The history continues through the exam; don't assume old records are still current; stay in control of time.
Suggested order: general info, LEE, RFV, OH, FOH, GH, FMH, symptom check, occupation and lifestyle.
Return to the reason for visit at the end and reassure where you can.

decks.title: History and symptoms seminar
decks.summary: The in-class seminar: feedback from the retinoscopy and subjective assessment, an example of a well-recorded history, common pitfalls, and data on the opening question.
takeaways: Assessment feedback: the commonest lost marks were for over-minusing; always write powers to two decimal places with a sign, and keep cards legible.
Over 70% of diagnoses can come from a good history.
Patients' uninterrupted talking time is typically about 30 seconds to a minute.
A good record is in pen, legible, complete (including negatives) and shows follow-up questions.

decks.title: Practitioner health and wellbeing
decks.summary: Why your own health matters to patient safety: stress and burnout in optometry, sources of support, fitness to practise and to train, declaring health conditions to the GOC, HEOPS medical fitness standards, and conditions that can affect safe practice. Includes the brief for the portfolio task that signs off GOC outcome 5.6.
takeaways: GOC outcome 5.6: understand how to maintain your own health to stay safe and effective. The portfolio task (about 1,000 words, with references) is the final sign-off.
Fitness to practise means having the skills, knowledge, health and character to work safely.
Declare a health condition to the GOC only if it currently affects your fitness to practise or train; give the condition, date of diagnosis and treatment. Insight matters.
HEOPS: reduced stereopsis doesn't bar you from training; colour deficiency is unlikely to; field defects may affect competencies.
Help: AOP peer support line, personal and senior tutors, Aston Mental Health and Wellbeing and Counselling services, and your GP.

outline.title: Stress in optometry
points: Stress is when demands seem to exceed your resources; signs can be emotional, mental or behavioural.
AOP survey (Aston, 2016): stress driven by long hours, time pressure, physical strain and lack of support; employers, part-timers and the independent sector reported less.
Recent research: distress and anxiety in optometrists are higher than in the general population; 17% had treatment for a mental health condition in the past year.
Five ways to wellbeing: connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, give.

outline.title: Students
points: Risks: perfectionism, money, workload, travel, other commitments, isolation and finding a placement.
Support: tutors, peers and staff, and Aston's wellbeing and counselling services.

outline.title: Fitness to practise and train
points: The GOC investigates serious concerns, such as poor performance, health affecting work, misconduct, being impaired at work, dishonesty or convictions.
Anyone can raise a concern; registrants declare fitness on registration each year and can declare at any time.
HEOPS covers mobility, vision, hearing, speech, skin, loss of consciousness, neurodiversity and mental health.

outline.title: Conditions affecting safe practice
points: Alcohol dependence, drug misuse (about 10–15% of health professionals, similar to the general population), mental health conditions and other medical conditions.
Ask whether a condition affects safe practice now.

outline.title: Portfolio task
points: Three questions, about 1,000 words in total, with references; failing the GOC-required parts fails the task.
Drop-in help sessions run in weeks 10 and 11.

decks.title: Tear film and contact lenses
decks.summary: The lacrimal system (secretion, distribution and drainage), the lipid, aqueous and mucin layers and what's in them, blinking, osmolarity, and the clinical tests for tear quantity, quality and stability, with how meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis affect lens wear.
takeaways: Lipid comes from the meibomian glands and glands of Zeis and Moll; aqueous from the main and accessory (Krause, Wolfring) lacrimal glands; mucin from goblet cells and corneal epithelium.
The lipid layer (0.1–0.2 µm) slows evaporation; the aqueous layer is about 7 µm; mucin (about 0.05 µm) makes the surface wettable.
Tear volume about 7 µl, made at about 1.2 µl/min, turned over every 5 minutes; blink rate about 12/min, lower when reading or using a computer.
Partial blinks cause 3 and 9 o'clock staining in rigid lens wearers.
Assess quantity (Schirmer, phenol red thread, meniscus height), stability (TBUT, NIBUT), lipid (Tearscope interference), damage (staining) and symptoms (e.g. OSDI).

outline.title: Why tears matter in contact lens practice
points: Dry eye symptoms: reduced wearing time, discomfort late in the day or in some environments, irritation, grittiness, soreness, tiredness.
Secretory system: lipid, aqueous and mucin sources.

outline.title: The three layers
points: Lipid: wax and cholesterol esters with some polar lipids; seen as interference fringes; reduces evaporation.
Aqueous: ions for osmotic balance, glucose, metabolites, serum proteins and lacrimal proteins (lysozyme, lipocalin, lactoferrin, IgA), vitamin A, and cells.
Lysozyme attacks bacteria and is drawn to negatively charged (ionic) lenses; proteins denature on hydrophobic lens surfaces.
Mucin: glycoproteins that make the epithelium wettable and stop bacteria sticking.

outline.title: Distribution and drainage
points: Blinking spreads tears; the lower meniscus is a reservoir. Blink rate rises with conversation, anxiety, tiredness and dry environments; falls with reading, hard tasks and screens.
Orbicularis closes the lids; levator (with Müller's muscle) opens the upper lid.
Drainage through puncta, canaliculi and the nasolacrimal duct, driven by the lid pump; about 10% of aqueous evaporates.

outline.title: Structure, function and osmolarity
points: Several models of tear structure, from three separate layers to a mucoaqueous gel under lipid.
Functions: optical surface, nutrition, waste removal, preventing drying, lubrication, antibacterial.
Open-eye osmolarity about 315 mOsm/kg; reflex tearing lowers it.

outline.title: Assessment and lid disease
points: Schirmer strips (only useful for comparison) and phenol red threads, meniscus height, rose bengal and lissamine green, fluorescein TBUT (which adds volume), NIBUT, Tearscope interference patterns, debris, lid wiper and meibomian gland checks.
Rose bengal stains dead or degenerate cells and areas lacking mucin; dry-eye staining occurs in about a third of soft lens wearers.
Meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis destabilise the lipid layer and cause dry, itchy eyes and lens intolerance.

decks.title: Tear film: test your knowledge
decks.summary: Two short-answer questions (ocular surface dyes; dry eye tests and what each measures) and three MCQs. The answer sheet is 'Mgmt_CLB_04_CLB _Tears_test your knowledge_Ans.docx'. The SAQs and two of the MCQs are in the tear film topic; the tear-thickness MCQ is left out because its answer couldn't be confirmed from the slides.
takeaways: Dyes: fluorescein, rose bengal, lissamine green.
Glands of Moll contribute to the lipid layer.
TBUT measures stability, not secretion.

decks.title: Visual fields 1
decks.summary: The normal visual field and hill of vision, how to describe defects, and how the arrangement of nerve fibres from retina to striate cortex lets you work out where a lesion is: retinal, optic nerve, chiasmal (pituitary adenoma, meningioma, craniopharyngioma), tract, LGN, radiation and cortical defects.
takeaways: Normal monocular field: about 60° up and nasally, 70° down, 100° temporally. The blind spot is 15° temporal and 1.5° below the horizontal, 5.5° wide and 7.5° high.
Scotoma: focal loss, relative (some light seen) or absolute. Diffuse loss is a general depression.
Retinal nerve fibre damage gives arcuate scotomas and nasal steps that respect the horizontal midline.
Chiasmal compression (most often pituitary adenoma) gives bitemporal defects; a junctional scotoma means compression where the optic nerve meets the chiasm (Wilbrand's knee).
Further back along the pathway, homonymous defects become more congruent. Stroke is the commonest cause of homonymous hemianopia.

outline.title: The normal field
points: Limited by brow, nose and cheek; central field 0–30°, peripheral beyond.
Field and retina are inverted and reversed.
Traquair's 'hill of vision in a sea of blindness'; the physiological blind spot is the temporal projection of the optic disc.

outline.title: Describing defects
points: Focal (scotoma, relative or absolute) or diffuse (depression).
By shape: quadrantanopia, hemianopia, altitudinal, arcuate, nasal step, junctional; by location: central, paracentral, peripheral.
Between eyes: homonymous (same side) or heteronymous; congruence (how well they match) helps place the lesion.

outline.title: Retinal causes
points: Nerve fibre layer: arcuate, paracentral and nasal step defects; papillomacular bundle damage gives central loss.
Optic disc drusen: enlarged blind spot and inferonasal arcuate defects. Coloboma: usually inferior, mimics glaucoma, stable.
Vascular: deep, sharp-edged defects respecting the horizontal. Also vigabatrin toxicity and AMD.

outline.title: Optic nerve and chiasm
points: Intraorbital nerve lesions tend to hit the papillomacular bundle; optic nerve sheath meningioma reduces VA and causes disc swelling then atrophy.
At the chiasm nasal fibres cross (inferior nasal fibres loop through Wilbrand's knee); temporal fibres don't.

Pituitary adenoma: bitemporal loss (often upper temporal first), reduced VA, disc pallor and colour defects. Craniopharyngioma presses from above. Prefixed and postfixed chiasms (10% each) change the pattern.

outline.title: Behind the chiasm
points: Tract lesions are rare and incongruent; LGN lesions are usually vascular (e.g. hourglass defects).
Optic radiations: compression or more often vascular damage. Stroke causes field loss in a half to three-quarters of victims, most often homonymous hemianopia; recovery, if any, is within a month.
About 80% of striate cortex serves the central 30°; macular sparing is hard to show without a 10-2 grid or Amsler.
Perimetry is indicated for neurological investigation and glaucoma, and should be done routinely where possible.

decks.title: Pain in or around the eye tutorial
decks.summary: A case tutorial on eye pain. The slides are mostly case-record images; the text points to pupil clues (distorted in iritis, oval and mid-dilated in angle closure), the conditions in the differential (orbital cellulitis, orbital tumour, iritis), and the usual reminders about questions not asked, tests not done and conditions with more than one referral urgency.
takeaways: Distorted pupil: iritis. Oval, mid-dilated pupil: acute angle closure.
Pain with proptosis: think orbital cellulitis or orbital tumour.
Check what the record leaves out and match referral urgency to the findings.

decks.title: Headache tutorial
decks.summary: A case tutorial on headache. The slides are mostly case-record images; the referral slide contrasts chronic daily headache (CDH) and episodic tension-type headache (ETTH). Use with the headache questions in the history and symptoms lecture.
takeaways: Follow up any headache with LOFTSEA even if the patient thinks it isn't visual.
Only a small proportion of headaches are due to refractive or binocular problems.
Know the difference between chronic daily headache and episodic tension-type headache for referral.

decks.title: Experimental design
decks.summary: Designing a behavioural experiment, worked through with a darts-and-alcohol example: experimental and null hypotheses, one- and two-tailed predictions, independent, dependent, confounding and extraneous variables, floor and ceiling effects, placebos and blinding, within- versus between-subjects designs, and controlling order effects.
takeaways: We test the null hypothesis because a hypothesis can be falsified but never proven, and there is only one null to test against.
One-tailed: you predict a direction (alcohol makes darts worse). Two-tailed: any change.

A confounding variable changes with the independent variable, so an experiment with one is wasted. A placebo removes the confound of knowing your condition; double-blind means the experimenter doesn't know either.
Floor effect: the task is too hard to show a drop. Ceiling effect: too easy to show a change. Pilot studies set the levels.
Within-subjects designs are usually better; control order effects (fatigue, learning) by counterbalancing or randomised blocks.

outline.title: Hypotheses
points: Turn a vague idea ('alcohol makes you clumsy') into a testable statement.
H1: alcohol degrades visuo-motor performance; H0: it doesn't. Adding 'improves' as H2 makes it two-tailed.
Why a null: you can't prove 'all moorhens have green feet' but one counter-example disproves it; and you can compare data with a mean of zero, but not with every possible size of effect.

outline.title: Variables
points: Independent (manipulated; its levels are conditions, often including a control), dependent (measured), confounding and extraneous.
Not every experiment needs a control condition, e.g. measuring the contrast sensitivity function across spatial frequencies.
Choose task difficulty to avoid floor and ceiling effects; adding a second independent variable (distance) makes a two-factor design.

outline.title: Confounds and extraneous variables
points: Handing over a drink only in the alcohol condition is a confound: participants know which condition they're in. Use a placebo (single-blind) or blind the experimenter too (double-blind).
Hold extraneous variables (temperature, lighting, time of day) constant so they don't become confounds.

outline.title: Participants and order
points: Random sampling is hard; avoid obviously biased samples.
Within-subjects cancels out differences between people; between-subjects is needed for sex or age comparisons or very long experiments.
Order effects: fatigue or learning. Counterbalance (half each order) or, with many levels, run randomised blocks.

decks.title: Handout 9 and 10: experimental design and statistics
decks.summary: Prof Meese's notes for weeks 9 and 10: participant designs and order effects, visual psychophysics, one- and two-tailed significance, the t-test, ANOVA, descriptive statistics and the meaning of n, large-n versus small-n studies and data independence, non-parametric tests, and a golden rule for experimental design.
takeaways: Psychophysics is the main method for measuring human sensory performance.
The t-test compares two means; ANOVA handles more than two levels or several factors.
Be clear what n means (participants, trials or measurements) and keep data points independent.
Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests are available when data don't meet parametric assumptions.

decks.title: Week 9 test your knowledge: experimental design
decks.file: VSE Week 9 Experimental design Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Four questions on experimental variables, reading a data figure, confounds and floor effects. Three are in the research design quiz; the figure question isn't, because the figure didn't come through in the text copy.
takeaways: 'Experimental variable' is another name for the independent variable.
With a confound, the true relationship could even be the opposite way round.
A floor effect leaves no room for the measure to drop further.

decks.title: Aspheric lenses
decks.summary: What aspheric lenses are and why they're used, how a surface's built-in astigmatism cancels oblique astigmatism, conic sections and p values, sag and thickness calculations, field plots for high-plus lenses, low-power aspherics, atoroidal surfaces, verification and dispensing.
takeaways: An aspheric surface is rotationally symmetrical but not spherical (so toric and progressive surfaces don't count).
Used first (c.1909) for high plus over +7.00 D, where no spherical best form exists; since about 1980 to make low powers flatter and thinner without losing off-axis quality.
p values: circle 1, prolate ellipse 0 to 1, parabola 0, hyperbola below 0, oblate ellipse above 1. Lower p flattens more.
Sag x = y² ÷ [r₀ + √(r₀² − py²)]; thickness: tc + S2 = te + S1.
Centre aspherics carefully, never decentre them to make prism, and use atoroidal designs for cylinders over about 1.50 D.

outline.title: Why aspherics
points: One aspheric surface (usually the front) plus a spherical or toric surface.
Tscherning: no two-sphere solution free of oblique astigmatism above +7.00 D. An aspheric front whose tangential power falls faster than sagittal power cancels it.
For a +12.00 lens the spherical form gives about +2.00 D of oblique cyl at 30°; a suitable asphere removes it, leaving a small negative MOE.

outline.title: Conic surfaces
points: Defined by apical radius r₀ and p value; p below 1 means the surface flattens away from the axis.
rs = √[r₀² + (1 − p)y²]; rt = rs³ ÷ r₀².
Example, 70 mm diameter, r₀ 80 mm, n 1.5: sag 8.06 mm (sphere), 7.85 (p 0.5), 7.66 (p 0), 7.04 (p −2). Flatter means thinner, with more surface astigmatism to cancel oblique astigmatism.

outline.title: Worked sag example and field plots
points: +2.00 / −10.00 lens, front p = 0, 40 mm, tc 1.5 mm: front sag 0.8 mm, back 4.174 mm, edge 4.87 mm.
+10.00 lens at 35°: p 1.0 gives OAE 2.29; p 0.4 gives zero MOE (Percival-like); p 0 gives near-zero OAE (point focal-like); p −4 overcorrects.

outline.title: Aphakic and low-power aspherics
points: Aphakic forms: full-aperture and lenticular conic or polynomial, blended lenticulars, zonal aspherics.
Under 6 D, aspheric fronts let you use flatter forms with best-form optics; biggest benefit for plus lenses.
Aspheric plus high index saves thickness twice: flatter curves, then more asphericity to correct them.

outline.title: Verification and dispensing
points: A lens measure reads the same everywhere on a sphere; on an aspheric plus front the reading drops towards the edge (a minus aspheric reads more towards the edge).
Atoroidal surfaces give different p values in each meridian for cylinders over about 1.50 D.
Centre carefully so primary gaze is through the centre, and never induce prism by decentring.

decks.title: Aspheric lens worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Six worksheets: sag, edge thickness and edge surface powers; sags and thickness in a real frame; short questions on aspherics; reading a field plot; a high-plus patient unhappy with cheap second spectacles; and an extended Ray Trace exercise. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_9_Aspheric lenses worksheet answers_EH.pptx'; the main ones are worked through in the aspherics topic.
takeaways: Use r₀ = (n′ − n) ÷ F with the index after the surface as n′ (so a back surface has a negative numerator).
Glazing with the PD matching the frame centres can save over a millimetre of centre thickness.
Choose p for zero MOE (better for presbyopes) or near-zero OAE with negative MOE (non-presbyopes can accommodate).

decks.title: Selection and safe use of diagnostic drugs
decks.file: Mgmt_PaP_9_Selection & Safe Use of Diagnostic Drugs_PBB.pptx
decks.summary: Using diagnostic drops safely and within your competence: what to explain and ask before instilling, the 4D check, what to record, pre- and post-dilation checks for angle closure, cycloplegic examinations, and precautions with topical anaesthetics.
takeaways: Before drops: explain why, what they'll do and how long they last; ask about previous reactions; get consent (or assent).
4D check at the patient's shoulder: Drug, Dose, Date (expiry), Dispose.
Record drug, concentration and number of drops, which eye, batch number and expiry, plus all advice given.

Tropicamide is the mydriatic of choice (add phenylephrine for more dilation). Angle closure risk is about 1 in 5,000; check angles and IOP before and after, and refer suspected angle closure to eye casualty as an emergency.
Cyclopentolate for cycloplegic refraction: record VA and a dry refraction first, and recheck vision with the result once it wears off (24–48 hours).

outline.title: Before you instil anything
points: Only use drugs within your competence and after all the necessary checks.
Explain why, what and for how long; ask about past reactions; get consent; warn first-timers of possible effects.
4D test at the shoulder: drug, dose, date, dispose.

outline.title: Dilation
points: Tropicamide first choice; phenylephrine for more profound dilation.
Before: van Herick (or gonioscopy, shadow test, AS-OCT), IOP, and symptoms of sub-acute closure. After: angles and IOP again.
Don't dilate with an iris-clip lens. Advise sunglasses and no driving, cycling or machinery; refer suspected angle closure as an emergency and inform the GP.

outline.title: Cycloplegia
points: Cyclopentolate is the drug of choice, usually in children, where angle and IOP checks are hard; in young adults check them before and after.
Record VA and a dry refraction first, watch for adverse reactions, and check vision with the prescription once the drug has worn off, making sure the patient isn't fogged.
Check BNF contraindications for antimuscarinics.

outline.title: Topical anaesthetics
points: Ask about previous reactions; they are potentially highly toxic.
Always check for staining after the examination.

decks.title: Record keeping and the Xeyex system
decks.summary: Why records matter legally and professionally, what GOC standards and outcome 4.12 require, an introduction to Xeyex (the Aston Eye Clinic's electronic record) using a practice case, and how to structure a record as subjective findings, objective findings, assessment and plan. (Use the training login given in the session; it isn't reproduced here.)
takeaways: A record is a legal document: in a GOC enquiry it is the first thing looked at, and decisions rest on what's written.
Records must be clear, accurate, contemporaneous and accessible, with history, findings, consent, referrals, advice and who did any delegated task.
Know data protection, freedom of information and Subject Access Requests.
A good record lets a reader see the Subjective findings, Objective findings, Assessment and Plan.
Check that every finding has what it needs, e.g. a near add with N-number, working distance and range.

outline.title: Why records matter
points: GOC outcome 4.12 and the 19 Standards of Practice.
Records protect you and the patient and are central to any GOC enquiry.

outline.title: Xeyex practice case
points: Entering history, VA, cover test, subjective Rx with near add and range, slit lamp and fundus findings.
Spot missing information (e.g. a near VA without a working distance). Can a +1.75 add with a 23–63 cm range be used for a screen at 70 cm?
Fundus biomicroscopy still matters: widefield imaging and a 90 D lens without dilation can show peripheral lattice with laser marks.

outline.title: Reading and writing a good record
points: Subjective: general information, complaint, ocular, general and family history, visual demands.
Objective: all examination findings. Assessment: link the findings to the complaint (e.g. 6/18 with no pathology suggests about −1.00 D).
Plan: spectacles, contact lenses, vision therapy, drugs, advice or referral, with a prognosis.

decks.title: Visual fields 2
decks.summary: How fields are measured: kinetic versus static perimetry, Goldmann sizes and intensities, decibels and thresholds, full-threshold, fast and suprathreshold strategies, choosing a test grid, and the Esterman test and driving standards, including its limitations.
takeaways: Kinetic: a moving target from non-seeing to seeing (about 4°/s) maps isopters; good for deep loss and residual fields. Static: fixed positions, brightness varied; more sensitive to shallow and small defects.
Confrontation is insensitive (about 63% overall) and only a gross check.
1 dB = 0.1 log unit; 0 dB is the perimeter's brightest stimulus; dB scales differ between machines.
Full threshold (4-2 dB staircase, about 13 minutes an eye) quantifies; fast strategies take about 8 minutes; suprathreshold (about 5 dB above threshold) screens but can miss defects up to 4 dB deep.
UK driving: number plate at 20 m (about 6/9–6/12) and 120° of horizontal field, tested with the Esterman, which isn't adjusted for eccentricity or age.

outline.title: Kinetic perimetry and confrontation
points: Kinetic: Goldmann bowl, Bjerrum screen, confrontation; isopters join points of equal sensitivity.
Static: independent of reaction time, more sensitive; automated is better than manual.
Shahinfar et al. (1995): confrontation detected 51% of arcuate scotomas and 90% of hemianopias.

outline.title: Stimuli, thresholds and strategies
points: Goldmann sizes 0 to V; intensity in apostilbs and dB.
Threshold is the 50% probability of seeing; it fluctuates (short-term fluctuation).
Full threshold: start from an age norm, cross threshold twice (4 dB then 2 dB). Fast: one crossing (3 dB), quicker but more variable.

outline.title: Suprathreshold screening and grids
points: Gradient-adapted suprathreshold strategies follow the shape of the hill of vision and test many points quickly; the Henson perimeter shows several stimuli at once.
24-2 and 30-2 (77 points, 6° apart) for glaucoma, cataract and neurology; 10-2 (69 points, 2° apart) for the macula; Esterman for driving.

outline.title: Driving and the Esterman test
points: European standards vary (e.g. 120° in several countries, 140° in Switzerland and the Netherlands).
Esterman: binocular, a 10 dB stimulus, points seen or missed, scored as a functional vision score that weights central loss more.
Its stimulus isn't adjusted for eccentricity or age, so older drivers may miss more points.

decks.title: Contact lens materials and prescribing
decks.summary: Where contact lenses fit among ways of correcting refraction, wear modalities and the advantages of disposables, cost and prescribing trends, why people drop out, oxygen permeability and transmissibility, wettability, and contact lens optics (back vertex power, vertex distance, accommodation, aberrations).
takeaways: Disposables (from 1987) mean fewer deposit problems and unscheduled visits, higher-water lenses, spares, simpler care and better patient management.
About 4.75 million people in the UK wear lenses; 20–50% of wearers drop out, half of them because of discomfort.
Wettability is measured in vitro by sessile drop, Wilhelmy plate or captive bubble, and in vivo by tear break-up.
Measure contact lens BVP with a small focimeter stop; correct spectacle power for vertex distance: Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − dFsp).
Myopes accommodate more with contact lenses than spectacles (presbyopia may show sooner); hyperopes accommodate less.

outline.title: Options, modalities and trends
points: Options include spectacles, refractive surgery, soft, rigid and ortho-k lenses, IOLs and corneal implants.
Conventional, planned replacement and disposable wear; cost rises with optical complexity, replacement frequency and material technology.
Let patients weigh cost, convenience and visual benefit; include solutions and chair time.

outline.title: The market and drop-out
points: The UK is Europe's largest market (about 19.5% of European wearers, over £700m).
20–50% stop wearing lenses: discomfort, inconvenience, cost and complications. Reducing drop-out by 1% is worth about $120 million worldwide.

outline.title: Physical properties
points: Dk (permeability) is a material property measured at 34°C; Dk/t (transmissibility) depends on thickness.
Wettability: contact angle by sessile drop, Wilhelmy plate or captive bubble; tear break-up on the eye.

outline.title: Optical properties
points: Fewer design freedoms, narrow index range, and soft lenses conform to the cornea; rigid optics are more predictable but the lens moves.
Indices: tears 1.336, cornea 1.376, keratometer 1.3375.
Spectacle aberrations (oblique astigmatism, distortion, TCA) grow with power and lens size; contact lenses move with the eye so prism effects don't apply in the same way.

decks.title: Contact lens materials and prescribing: test your knowledge
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_09_CLB_test your knowledge_CL materials and prescribing_Q.docx
decks.summary: A short-answer question on the advantages of disposable lenses and three MCQs. The answer sheet is 'Mgmt_CLB_09_CLB _Test your knowledge_CL materials and prescribing_Ans.docx'. The SAQ and two MCQs are in the topic; the prescribing-trend MCQ is left out because the answer depends on charts that didn't come through in the text.
takeaways: EOP is an oxygen measure, not a wettability test.
Hyperopes accommodate less with contact lenses than with spectacles.

decks.title: Visual field loss tutorial
decks.summary: A case tutorial on a patient reporting loss of part of their vision. The text slides profile the causes to tell apart: retinal detachment (macula on or off), acute and progressive optic neuropathy, wet and dry macular degeneration, glaucoma, brain disease, migraine and TIA.
takeaways: Retinal detachment: a curtain over the vision, low IOP (under 10 mmHg), tobacco dust (Shafer's sign), elevated pale retina; macula-on is more urgent to save central vision.
Brain disease: transient bilateral blur, headaches worse lying down, neurological symptoms, swollen discs, and homonymous defects respecting the vertical midline.
TIA: seconds of blurred vision or sparkles with neurological symptoms; everything else normal.
Wet AMD: sudden one-eyed blur with drusen, haemorrhage, a grey-green membrane, exudates and oedema; urgency depends on how recent.
Glaucoma: gradual, painless, repeatable loss respecting the horizontal midline.

decks.title: Basic statistics and analysis
decks.summary: Analysing the darts experiment: means, standard deviation and standard error, reading error bars, what p means, statistical versus clinical significance, one- versus two-tailed tests and registered reports, ANOVA for more conditions, and why people judge risk badly.
takeaways: SD describes spread; SE = SD ÷ √n. Error bars on plotted means usually show ±1 SE.
p is the probability of results this extreme (or more) if the null hypothesis were true. p ≤ 0.05 is significant; p ≤ 0.01 highly significant.
Significant isn't proven, and it isn't necessarily clinically important.
Decide one- or two-tailed before collecting data; switching afterwards is cheating, which registered reports prevent.
Use a t-test for two conditions and ANOVA (F ratio) for more conditions or factors.

outline.title: Descriptive statistics
points: The means of 9, 10, 11 and of 1, 10, 19 are both 10, but the spreads differ.
SD is the formal measure of spread; SE (SD ÷ √n) describes how precisely the mean is known.

outline.title: Looking at results
points: Overlapping SE bars: the difference in means tells you little. Clear separation: probably meaningful.
A significant difference may still be too small to matter scientifically or clinically.

outline.title: Inferential statistics
points: The t-test gives t and, more usefully, p (between 0 and 1).
If significant we reject H0 and 'have evidence to support' H1; chance can never be ruled out.
A two-tailed test splits 5% between both tails; a one-tailed test puts it all in one, so a result can be significant one-tailed but not two-tailed. ANOVA handles more levels and factors.

outline.title: Judging risk
points: '100 times the risk' means little without the baseline: 1 in 100 million becomes 1 in a million, far below the roughly 1 in 2,500 yearly chance of death or serious injury on UK roads.
Every lottery combination, including 1–6, is equally unlikely; intuition handles very big and very small numbers badly. Relevant to practice risks like a trip hazard.

decks.title: Week 10 test your knowledge: statistics
decks.file: VSE Week 10 Stats and analysis Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Five multiple-choice questions on significance, p values, ANOVA, descriptive statistics and registered reports. Four are in the statistics quiz (the p-value question is left out because two options are arguably true); answers are worked out from the lecture.
takeaways: Not significant one-tailed in the predicted direction means not significant two-tailed either.
ANOVA can look at main effects and interactions across three factors.
t is an inferential statistic, not a descriptive one.
Registered reports stop one-tailed testing being chosen after the fact.

decks.title: Prescribing tips and counselling
decks.summary: Deciding the final prescription (listening to and involving the patient, myopes, hyperopes, phorias, big changes, cylinders, anisometropia, high powers, low vision adds and vertex distance), small refractive errors and small changes, and how to counsel and record advice. Ends with sample MCQs and an SAQ with answers.
takeaways: 'If it ain't broke, don't fix it': a happy patient wanting a new frame may be best with their old Rx.
Don't over-plus myopes; give hyperopes only enough plus to remove symptoms (full correction for presbyopes, esotropia and esophoria).
More minus can decompensate esophoria; more plus can decompensate exophoria.
Over 25, avoid changing by more than ±0.75 D; partial cylinder changes reduce non-tolerance (about 2% of exams lead to a recheck, often from cylinder changes, especially oblique ones).
Record your advice; standard recall is 2 years (1 year for children and the elderly); never disparage a previous optometrist.

outline.title: What to prescribe
points: Listen: a myope who sees better with glasses pushed closer needs more minus; a hyperope who pushes them away needs more plus.
Compare old and new in a trial frame; ask if they'd like new glasses. A presbyopic myope may like slight distance under-correction.

Myopes: err towards slight over-minus (6 m chart = +0.17 D; night myopia). Hyperopes: partial correction (about ½ to ¾ if manifest); check tolerance of extra plus before cycloplegia; consider bifocals if needed.

outline.title: Big changes and cylinders
points: Beaver Dam: adult refraction changes slowly, so a big change needs explaining.
Over 25, don't change by more than ±0.75 D; consider staging the change.

Consider not prescribing 0.25 DC. Make partial changes if the cyl changes by more than 0.75 DC or the axis by more than 30° (up to 1.00 DC), 15° (1.00–2.00 DC) or 7.5° (over 2.00 DC); adjust the sphere and try it in a trial frame.

outline.title: Special cases
points: Anisometropia under 1.00 D rarely causes aniseikonia; contact lenses often help; a balance lens may suit long-standing dense amblyopia.
Presbyopic anisometropia (e.g. after cataract surgery): reduce by about a third, minimise BVD and thickness, match base curves, consider iseikonic lenses or contact lenses.
Over 3.00 D, match base curves, CD, BVD and material. Low vision adds above +2.50 bring work closer. Correct for vertex distance (F²/1000 per mm, or the exact formula).

outline.title: Small errors and small changes
points: No symptoms, no prescription. Prescribe more readily for detailed work, detail-focused people, clear subjective improvement, or to compensate a phoria; a trial Rx can be diagnostic.
GOC standard 16.3: don't let targets or incentives affect judgement.
No change in Rx: ask if they'd still like another pair (new frame, damage, spare, task-specific).

outline.title: Counselling
points: Cover the chief complaint, ocular health, the need for Rx and recall, in order of importance to the patient, in plain language, with leaflets or diagrams.
Reassure when no cause is found ('advised H/A not ocular'); explain when to wear the Rx, likely adaptation and prognosis.
The previous optometrist may have changed a cylinder or under-corrected on purpose (GOC 13.6: no disparaging comments). Recall 2 years, or 1 for children and the elderly; explain shorter recalls.

decks.title: Prescribing tips and counselling: question answers
decks.summary: Answers to the two MCQs and the vertex distance SAQ from the lecture; all are in the prescribing topic.
takeaways: It can be sensible to put the old prescription in a new frame.
Extra plus can decompensate exophoria in a young patient.
+5.50 moved 3 mm closer changes by only about 0.10 D, so the glazed powers stay the same.

decks.title: Contact lens complications
decks.summary: Microorganisms and how lens wear affects host defences, then the main adverse events: hypoxic changes, microbial keratitis, corneal infiltrative events (CLPU, CLARE, IK), contact lens discomfort and dry eye, papillary conjunctivitis, SEALs and erosions, with incidences, risk factors and management.
takeaways: About a third of wearers have some adverse event.
Microbial keratitis: about 1–2 per 10,000 daily wearers per year, about 20 per 10,000 with overnight wear. Risks: poor hand hygiene, overnight wear, smoking, water, male sex.
Daily disposables don't reduce the absolute risk of MK but cases seem milder with less vision loss.
Corneal infiltrative events: 0–0.4% a year with daily disposables, 2.5–7% with overnight reusables.
Contact lens dry eye affects 15–55% of wearers; manage by removing other causes, then changing care, modality, material or tear support.

outline.title: Microbes and host defence
points: Gram-positive (e.g. Staphylococcus, Streptococcus) versus Gram-negative (e.g. Pseudomonas, which has an outer membrane).
Daily wear increases lid and conjunctival bacteria, partly from the case.
Lens wear alters epithelial function (Dk/t dependent) and reduces PMNs and sIgA; most adverse responses come from bacterial colonisation of lenses.

outline.title: Microbial keratitis
points: Presumed MK: stromal infiltrate over 1 mm, more than mild pain, plus AC reaction, discharge or a positive culture.
Rapid pain, redness and discharge; ulcer with infiltrate, mucus and oedema.
Prevention: hand hygiene, replacement and compliance, no overnight wear; present early. Treatment: identify the organism, antimicrobials, cycloplegic, lubricants, later steroids.

outline.title: Inflammatory and mechanical events
points: CLPU: single round peripheral infiltrate up to 2 mm with overlying staining. CLARE: diffuse peripheral infiltration with small infiltrates, usually no staining. IK: anterior stromal infiltrates with staining.
CLPC: papillae on the upper tarsus. SEAL: grey-white arc in the superior cornea. Erosion: full-thickness epithelial loss.
Avoid overnight wear; peroxide systems or daily disposables help those with past CIEs or blepharitis.

outline.title: Contact lens discomfort and dry eye
points: CLIDE: symptoms only with lenses. CLADE: pre-existing dry eye in a lens wearer.

Rule out systemic and ocular disease and lens problems; then change care system, go daily disposable, change material or design, add lubricants, punctal plugs or omega-3, and avoid harsh environments.

outline.title: Papillary conjunctivitis and erosions
points: CLPC: probably immunological, more common with non-ionic hydrogels; frequent replacement helps.
Erosions: well-defined full-thickness epithelial loss.

decks.title: Contact lens complications: test your knowledge
decks.summary: Two short-answer questions (effects on host defences; toxic and allergic events) and three MCQs. The answer sheet is 'Mgmt_CLB_10_CLB _Test your knowledge_complications_Ans.docx'. The SAQs and two MCQs are in the complications topic; the 'which is Gram-positive' MCQ is left out because four of its options are Gram-positive.
takeaways: Gram-positive cell walls have no outer membrane.
An arc-shaped grey-white superior lesion is a SEAL.

decks.title: Drug legislation
decks.summary: The law on medicines for optometrists: the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 and the MHRA, POM, P and GSL categories, signed orders, medical devices, controlled drugs, the four levels of optometric practice (entry, additional supply, supplementary and independent prescribing), PGDs, self-prescribing and instillation by unregistered staff.
takeaways: The Human Medicines Regulations 2012 replaced the Medicines Act 1968; the MHRA enforces them.
Medicines are POM (prescription only), P (pharmacy) or GSL (general sale). Some drugs fall into more than one depending on pack size, strength and use.
Signed orders need your name, address and GOC number, the date, patient details if relevant, drug, quantity, form and strength, labelling directions and your original signature.
Contact lenses and solutions are class IIb medical devices; dye strips are class I.
Four levels: entry, additional supply, supplementary prescribing and independent prescribing; the last three need GOC-approved extra training.

outline.title: Framework and law
points: AFLUC: administration, formulation, legislation, utilisation, contraindication.
Medicine versus medical device; HMRs 2012 enforced by the MHRA via the Commission on Human Medicines; medicines are normally supplied from registered pharmacies.

outline.title: Categories
points: POM (about 4,500), P (about 1,200; anything not on the other lists), GSL (about 1,500; eye lotions are the main optometric example, but not drops or ointments).
Signed orders are needed for entry-level and additional supply drugs.
Medical devices: contact lenses and solutions (class IIb), dye strips (class I). Controlled drugs (Misuse of Drugs Act 1971) don't apply to optometric practice.

outline.title: Entry level and additional supply
points: Entry level P medicines include antazoline, chloramphenicol 0.5% for acute bacterial conjunctivitis, propamidine, sodium cromoglicate, lodoxamide, phenylephrine, fluorescein and rose bengal.

Additional supply covers non-sight-threatening conditions (allergic, infective, blepharitis, dry eye, superficial injury), e.g. ketotifen, olopatadine, acetylcysteine, polymyxin B, atropine, pilocarpine; supplied direct only in an emergency.
AS needs a postgraduate course and a supervised hospital placement.

outline.title: Prescribing and other rules
points: Supplementary prescribing: a voluntary partnership with a doctor under a clinical management plan (glaucoma, post-surgery).
Independent prescribing extends this. PGDs allow co-management with drugs outside these lists.
Avoid self-prescribing POMs; unregistered staff may instil drops only with the optometrist present and able to step in. Ignorance of the law is no excuse.

decks.title: Visual fields 3
decks.summary: Full threshold perimetry and the newer algorithms that speed it up (SITA, ZATA, GATE), choosing a grid, and controlling the things that spoil a field result: refractive correction, set-up, fixation, false positives and negatives, fatigue and learning.
takeaways: SITA uses prior knowledge (normal and glaucoma fields, neighbouring points, age) to estimate thresholds: SITA Standard matches full threshold in about 7 minutes; SITA Fast matches FASTPAC in about 4.
ZATA (Henson) and GATE (Octopus) can start from the patient's previous results.

Use the right near correction (Humphrey tests at 33 cm): full-aperture trial lenses, single vision or readers with cyl up to 1.00 DC; not bifocals, varifocals or tints. +4.00 blur cuts sensitivity by about 6 dB.
Watch for lens rim artefacts, head position and fixation (Heijl-Krakau blind spot checks or gaze tracking).
High false negatives exaggerate loss; high false positives hide it. Keep the order of eyes the same and allow breaks.

outline.title: Threshold algorithms
points: Full threshold allows statistical comparison with normals and progression analysis.
Bayesian methods: knowing something about what's likely speeds up the estimate (the balls-in-a-bag example).
Full threshold 13 min, FASTPAC 8 min, SITA Standard 7 min, SITA Fast 4 min; use the faster ones for routine patients and the more accurate when suspicious.

outline.title: Grids
points: 24-2 and 30-2 for glaucoma, cataract and neurology; 10-2 for the macula; Humphrey screening grids of 26, 68 or 136 points.

outline.title: Controlling artefacts
points: Correct for the test distance; contact lenses only for non-presbyopes.
Lens just clear of the lashes, head straight, comfortable posture.
False negatives (missing a stimulus brighter than threshold) and false positives (responding to nothing) measure reliability; fatigue and learning effects need controlling.

decks.title: Perceptual grouping and mid-level vision
decks.summary: How the visual system gets from local edges to objects: the Gestalt grouping rules, figure-ground and border ownership, competition between rules, Prägnanz, texture segmentation and contour linking, visual search (pop-out versus conjunction search), and an experiment showing grouping can use 3D depth, which breaks Marr's strictly feed-forward scheme.
takeaways: Gestalt rules: proximity, similarity, good continuation, closure, symmetry, common fate; Prägnanz says we see the simplest structure.
No rule always wins: proximity beats similarity in one display and loses in another.
V2 cells signal border ownership, which helps separate figure from ground.
Single-feature targets 'pop out' (parallel search, reaction time flat with distractors); conjunction targets need serial search (reaction time rises with distractors).
Enns and Rensink (1990): pop-out can depend on 3D orientation, so grouping isn't just a V1-level 2D process.

outline.title: Gestalt grouping
points: 'The whole is greater than the sum of the parts' (Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler).
Proximity, similarity, good continuation, closure, symmetry, amodal completion and common fate, with grouping and segmentation working together.

outline.title: Figure and ground, and competing rules
points: A dalmatian with no outline still segments from the background by similarity; Rubin's vase is ambiguous.
Border-ownership cells in V2 (Zhou et al., 2000).
Rows or columns? Proximity and similarity trade places, so there's no fixed order of precedence.

outline.title: Prägnanz
points: The 'law of good figure' or simplicity: we see the simplest possible structure.
But how do you measure simplicity? The Gestaltists described rather than explained; a real explanation should be programmable.

outline.title: Texture and contours
points: Oriented simple-cell filters provide the basis for texture segmentation.

Field, Hayes and Hess (1993): contours of aligned elements are easy to see, while equally regular non-aligned chains are hard, so vision has a built-in code for smooth contours (an 'association field').

outline.title: Visual search and Marr
points: Feature search (find the horizontal, find the green) is parallel; conjunction search (green and horizontal) is serial.
Marr's three stages: 2D features, surfaces, 3D objects, strictly feed-forward.
Enns and Rensink: search is nearly parallel for targets defined by 3D orientation, so depth affects grouping and Marr's strict scheme can't be right.

decks.title: Handout 11: perceptual grouping
decks.summary: Prof Meese's written notes for the perceptual grouping lecture.
takeaways: Read alongside the lecture: the Gestalt rules, figure-ground, texture, contour linking and visual search.

decks.title: Week 11 test your knowledge: perceptual grouping
decks.file: VSE Week 11 Perceptual grouping Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Three multiple-choice questions on common fate, border ownership and conjunction search, all in the grouping quiz (answers worked out from the lecture).
takeaways: Seeing a shape only when it moves is common fate.
Border ownership contributes to figure-ground segregation.
Conjunction search slows as distractors increase.

decks.title: Facial measurements and frame fitting
decks.summary: Every measurement you might take when dispensing: distance PD and mono PDs, near centration distance, pupillometers, multifocal and progressive heights, back vertex distance, pantoscopic and dihedral angles, and the Fairbanks facial measurement rule for custom frames, plus frame fitting.
takeaways: Measure PDs square-on, eyes level, at arm's length: at 40 cm each 1 mm of PD mismatch between you and the patient gives about 1/16 mm error.
Mono PDs for asymmetry, strabismus (occlude the other eye), progressives, aspherics and anisometropia.
Measure near centration distance in the spectacle plane, not near PD, after the frame is fitted.
BVD is needed for prescriptions over ±5.00 D (BS 2738-3), along the line of sight with zero pantoscopic tilt.
Free-form progressives also need pantoscopic angle (typically 8–12°) and dihedral (wrap) angle.

outline.title: PDs and near centration
points: Optical centres must sit in front of the pupils to avoid unwanted prism (discomfort, diplopia).
Ruler on the nose; patient looks at your left eye for their right pupil and your right eye for their left; read at matching points.

Mono PDs from the bridge centre to each pupil centre. Near CD is measured in the lens plane while the patient fixates a target at their working distance. Pupillometers use the first Purkinje image and avoid parallax.

outline.title: Multifocals and progressives
points: Square-on, eyes level, natural head posture, frame adjusted as worn.
Bifocal segment top at the lower limbus or lid (or as for an existing wearer; ask if they're happy); trifocal top at the bottom of the pupil; measure from the HCL.
Progressives: dot the pupil centres, remove and refit to check; pantoscopic angle 8–12°.

outline.title: BVD, pantoscopic and dihedral angles
points: BVD by distometer, ruler (estimate the back vertex or measure the front and subtract thickness), gauge or digital system.
Pantoscopic angle keeps the centre-of-rotation distance (and effective power) constant as the eye looks down.
Free-form lenses need mono PDs, heights, BVD, pantoscopic and dihedral angles.

outline.title: Facial measurement rule and frame fitting
points: For custom frames: PD, apical radius, head width, temple width (25 mm back), bridge projection, bridge height, splay and frontal angles, DBR at 10 and 15 mm below the crest, crest angle.
Choose the looser (larger) apical radius if between sizes.
Adjust and fit frames so measurements match the as-worn position.

decks.title: Facial measurement worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Two worksheets of short questions on measurement procedures, pantoscopic angle, free-form measurements, mono PDs in strabismus, BVD errors, frame markings and the facial measurement rule. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_11_Facial measurements worksheet answers_EH.pptx'; the main ones are in the facial measurements topic.
takeaways: Measure distance PDs but near CDs: converging eyes are closer together in the spectacle plane than the facial plane.
