Asymmetric mono PDs with a symmetrical centration can create differential prism in anisometropia.

decks.title: Binocular vision essentials and aligning prism
decks.summary: The motility test (muscle actions, yoke muscles, procedure and recording), the three stages of the cover test with worked eye movements, measuring deviations, and fixation disparity and aligning prism with the Mallett unit. Questions and answers come with the lecture.
takeaways: RAdSIn: recti adduct, superiors intort (so obliques abduct and inferiors extort).
Record normal motility as SAFE (smooth, accurate, full, extensive); otherwise note where diplopia or under- or overaction occurs.
Cover test stage 1 (cover/uncover the other eye) finds tropias; stage 2 (watch the uncovered eye recover) finds phorias; stage 3 (alternating) shows the total deviation and intermittent tropias.
Fixation disparity is a small misalignment within Panum's area, common with decompensated phoria; the prism that removes it is the aligning prism.
On the Mallett unit, use the smallest base-in prism for exo slip and base-out for eso slip; extra plus at near can remove an eso slip.

outline.title: Motility
points: Muscle actions (primary, secondary, tertiary), Sherrington's and Hering's laws, and the six cardinal positions testing yoke pairs.
Pen light at about 40 cm in an arc within the binocular field; lift the lids gently in downgaze.
If abnormal: where diplopia is worst, horizontal or vertical, which eye sees the outer image (the underacting eye).

outline.title: Cover test
points: The only objective test to tell phoria from tropia; done with habitual then optimal Rx at distance and near, target one line above the worse eye's VA.
Tropia direction: the eye moves out to fixate in esotropia, in for exotropia, down for hyper, up for hypo.
Estimate the size (1 cm at 1 m = 1Δ) or neutralise with a prism bar (base in for exo, base out for eso).

outline.title: Fixation disparity and aligning prism
points: Panum's fusional area and space allow single vision despite small misalignment.
Exo, eso and vertical slips; correct with the smallest prism that aligns the nonius strips, then check vertical and cyclo.
Practice questions and answers on Mallett findings, motility and muscle actions.

decks.title: BV essentials and aligning prism: questions and answers
decks.file: Ptnt_BVP_11_BV Essentials and Aligning prism QUESTIONS_AS.ppt.docx
decks.summary: Four MCQs and two short-answer questions (cover test movements in a right esotropia; using the Mallett unit). The answers file is 'Ptnt_BVP_11_BV Essentials and Aligning prism ANSWERS_AS.ppt.docx'. Three MCQs and both SAQs are in the binocular vision topics; the image-based prism question isn't, because the image didn't come through.
takeaways: Plus lenses at near can remove an eso slip.
Diplopia in down-and-left gaze points to LIR or RSO.
Inferior rectus: depression, extorsion and adduction.

decks.title: Visual fields 4: glaucoma and interpreting printouts
decks.summary: Glaucoma and fields: theories of damage, typical defects, and a step-by-step way to read a full-threshold printout (reliability, greyscale, global indices, total and pattern deviation maps, glaucoma hemifield test), with examples of normal, cataract, learning effect, glaucoma, homonymous and drug-toxicity fields.
takeaways: Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy with characteristic cupping and field loss; IOP isn't in the definition. Use IOP, disc and fields together, from age 35.
Unreliable: fixation losses over 20%, false negatives or false positives over 33%.
MD (mean deviation) reflects diffuse loss, e.g. cataract; PSD (and CPSD) reflects focal loss, e.g. glaucoma. Beyond about ±2 dB is usually abnormal.
Total deviation shows diffuse plus focal loss; pattern deviation removes the general depression to reveal focal loss.
The glaucoma hemifield test compares mirror-image upper and lower sectors.

outline.title: Glaucoma background
points: High-tension, normal-tension and low-tension glaucoma, and ocular hypertension; about 500,000 people in the UK.
Mechanical theory (IOP compresses the lamina) and vascular theory (reduced blood flow).
Disc: deepening and vertical enlargement of the cup, rim thinning, nasal vessel shift. Fields: paracentral scotomas, enlarged blind spot, nasal step, arcuate scotoma.

outline.title: Reading a printout
points: Reliability, numeric values (dB; 0 = brightest stimulus seen), greyscale.
Global indices: MD (diffuse), PSD/CPSD (focal), SF (variability; SITA doesn't calculate it).
Probability maps against age-matched normals (wider limits peripherally); glaucoma hemifield test outcomes.

outline.title: Worked examples
points: Normal with isolated points (repeat); cataract (high MD, low PSD); learning effect (apparent improvement at the second visit).
Early glaucoma (nasal step, significant maps but modest indices); advanced and very advanced glaucoma; cataract with glaucoma (pattern deviation reveals focal loss).
Homonymous quadrantanopia (post-chiasmal, incongruous, so probably near the chiasm); vigabatrin constriction failing the 120° driving standard.

decks.title: Adverse reactions 1: reporting
decks.summary: Terms for adverse reactions and their types, why ocular adverse reactions matter, the optometrist's role (monitor, detect, report), the Yellow Card scheme, sources of drug information, and judging how likely a reaction is.
takeaways: Adverse reaction: an unintended harmful effect of a correctly given drug. Side effect: a secondary unwanted effect. Allergic reaction: an immune response, an emergency.
Types A and B, plus C (continuing), D (delayed) and E (end-of-use).
Optometrists monitor, detect and report; reporting implies no criticism and the medication usually continues.

Report suspected reactions on a Yellow Card (MHRA) and inform the GP: all reactions to black-triangle drugs; serious reactions to established drugs, OTC and herbal products; with extra care for under-18s and the elderly.
Likelihood depends on the drug (dose, nature, interactions), the patient (age, with reactions peaking about 70; history; genetics) and their condition (chronic disease, metabolism).

outline.title: Terms and types
points: Sodium cromoglicate can be POM, P or GSL depending on use, strength and pack size.
Adverse reaction, side effect, allergic reaction, ocular adverse reaction (OAR).
The eye is small, specialised and pigmented, with vascular and avascular tissue and tears, so drugs can affect accommodation, pupils, phorias and dry eye.

outline.title: Monitoring, detecting and reporting
points: Optometrists see a large, wide age range regularly and can record baselines.
Yellow Card via the MHRA or BNF; inform the GP; emergency referral isn't usually needed.
Medical devices (contact lenses and care products, equipment) are reportable too.

outline.title: Information and probability
points: Sources: the patient, local prescribing, BNF (black triangle drugs), MIMS, MHRA Drug Safety Update, eMC, textbooks, emedINFO.
Weigh drug, patient and condition factors to estimate how likely a reaction is.

decks.title: Current UK market and contact lens modalities
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_11_Current UK market and CL modalities_DD -no vioceover.pptx
decks.summary: Wear modalities (daily, extended and continuous wear, planned replacement, daily disposables), how to decide between daily and extended wear, lens types, what drives replacement schedules, and market and prescribing trends.
takeaways: Extended wear: up to 6 nights and 7 days; continuous wear: up to 30 nights.
Daily versus extended wear depends on corneal status, risk factors, Rx, tear film, lids, environment and the individual. Any sign of corneal compromise rules out extended wear.
Choose modality for convenience, safety, comfort and the patient's understanding; explain the reasons as part of lens education.
The global market was about US$19.1 bn in 2024 (US about $6.1 bn), growing about 3.8% a year.
Daily disposables and silicone hydrogels make up a growing share of soft lens fits.

outline.title: Modalities and choosing
points: Signs of compromise (distortion, scars, infiltrates, microcysts, polymegethism, vascularisation, KPs) mean daily wear only.
Lens types: soft and GP (spherical, toric, multifocal), tinted, hybrid, scleral and prosthetic.
Replacement schedule factors: cost, convenience, management, therapeutic use and stock.

outline.title: Market and trends
points: Market size, in-clinic versus online sales.
International prescribing data (2000–2023) on wearer age and sex, silicone hydrogel share, daily disposables and replacement frequency.
Advantages of disposability and cost factors (as in week 9).

decks.title: Market and modalities: test your knowledge
decks.summary: A short-answer question on daily versus extended wear and two MCQs on market data. The answer sheet is 'Mgmt_CLB_11_CLB _Test your knowledge_market trend_Ans.docx'. The SAQ and the US revenue MCQ are in the topic; the silicone hydrogel share question isn't, because its answer depends on a chart that didn't come through.
takeaways: Corneal status, risk factors, Rx, tear film, lids, environment, individual characteristics.
2024 US market: over US$6 bn.

decks.title: Lightness perception
decks.summary: How we see the lightness of surfaces rather than the amount of light: luminance, illuminance and reflectance, lightness constancy through luminance ratios at edges and anchoring, the Craik-O'Brien-Cornsweet illusion and lightness contrast, and how shadows, penumbras and perceived 3D layout (Adelson's illusions, the crater and volcano) shape what we see.
takeaways: L = I × r: luminance is illuminance times reflectance. The retina only gets L, yet we judge r well (lightness constancy).
Brightness refers to light; lightness refers to surfaces.
Comparing ratios of neighbouring luminances gives relative reflectance; assuming the lightest area is white (anchoring) gives absolute lightness.
Ganglion cells respond to sudden luminance changes much more than gentle gradients, which explains the Craik-O'Brien-Cornsweet illusion.
Fuzzy edges (penumbras) are treated as shadows, not changes in surface; top-down interpretation of layout also matters, and works both ways.

outline.title: Terms and lightness constancy
points: Physical: reflectance, illuminance, luminance. Psychological: lightness, brightness.
A 100% and a 10% surface give luminances of 100 and 10 in bright light and 10 and 1 in dim light: the ratio stays 10:1.
Comparing ratios of neighbouring luminances gives relative reflectance.

outline.title: Ganglion cells, edges and illusions
points: Centre-surround cells compare adjacent regions; responding to ratios would signal relative reflectance at borders. Anchoring the lightest region to white gives absolute values.
A step edge gives a peak and a zero-crossing; a Craik-O'Brien-Cornsweet edge gives a similar response, so the two regions look different even though they're the same.
Lightness contrast: the same grey looks different on different surrounds.

outline.title: Shadows and higher-level effects
points: Shadows make luminance borders that aren't seen as changes in reflectance; blacking out a shadow's fuzzy penumbra makes it look like a dark stain.
Rule of thumb: don't apply lightness constancy across fuzzy borders.
Adelson's Argyle and checker-shadow illusions: perceived layout changes perceived lightness. The crater/volcano picture: perceived shading changes perceived layout.

decks.title: Handout 12: lightness
decks.summary: Prof Meese's written notes for the lightness perception lecture.
takeaways: Read alongside the lecture: L = I × r, lightness constancy, edge ratios and anchoring, illusions and shadows.

decks.title: Week 12 test your knowledge: lightness
decks.file: VSE Week 12 Lightness perception Test your knowledge.docx
decks.summary: Questions on the luminance equation and on which quantities are physical or psychological. Three are in the lightness quiz; the fourth isn't, because its question stem is missing from the Blackboard copy.
takeaways: r = L ÷ I.
Lightness is psychological, not a physical property.
Illuminance is physical; brightness is psychological.

decks.title: Occupational dispensing
decks.summary: Dispensing for work and leisure: task analysis (visibility versus visual capability), vision screening and occupational standards (police, drivers, trains, pilots), visual acuity nomograms, fields, colour vision, binocular vision and eye movements, VDU users, glare, eye injuries and PPE, lasers, sport and recreation.
takeaways: Visibility depends on the task (size, distance, lighting, contrast, colour, time, movement, glare); visual capability depends on the worker (VA, fields, binocular vision, colour, depth, adaptation).
For sustained tasks, VA should be about twice as good as the minimum the task needs.

Group 1 driving: number plate at 20 m, 6/12 binocularly, 120° horizontal field (50° each side) with no significant central defect. Group 2: 6/7.5 better eye, 6/60 worse, spectacles no stronger than ±8 D.
Employers must provide eye exams on request for regular VDU users and pay for basic spectacles needed only for VDU work.
Chemical injury is the most urgent ocular emergency: irrigate, don't pad, refer immediately.

outline.title: Task analysis and screening
points: Ask about working distances, gaze angles, detail size, contrast, colour, lighting, glare and hazards; get samples and measure distances.
Standards should separate competent from incompetent workers for that job.
Screening by modified clinical technique, instrument screeners or computer tests; benefits include fewer accidents and less absenteeism.

outline.title: Standards, VA and fields
points: Police (GOV.UK): corrected 6/12 each eye, 6/6 binocular, near 6/9, uncorrected 6/36, low-contrast 6/12, field 120° × 100°, monochromats rejected. MoD police differ.
A nomogram gives the VA needed from the size and distance of detail.
Fields: 60° up, 70° down, 95° temporal, 60° nasal; binocular overlap 120°. European driving standards vary.

outline.title: Colour, binocular vision, eye movements and VDUs
points: Colour matters for wiring, signals, dyes and design; some jobs specify the test, sometimes with secondary tests (e.g. the Holmes-Wright lantern).
Convergence is easiest below the horizontal, so put screen tops at eye level; standards usually exclude diplopia, not phorias.
Eye movements beyond about 15° bring in head movement; fatigue rises near capability limits.

outline.title: Glare and driving, trains and pilots
points: Distracting, discomforting and disabling glare (polarised filters help with disabling glare).
Group 1 and Group 2 driving standards; train drivers 6/9 and 6/12 with N8 and normal colour vision; pilots 6/6 binocular, 6/9 each eye, anisometropia and astigmatism no more than 2.00 D.
6/7.5 is needed to be sure of passing the number plate test; it's a criminal offence to drive below the standard.

outline.title: Safety, sport and dispensing
points: Occupational injuries are nearly a third of A&E eye injuries; employers do risk assessments and supply PPE; practices may adjust but not repair safety frames.
Mechanical, chemical, thermal, electrical and radiation injuries; laser classes 1 to 4.
Sport (squash and badminton are high risk), skiing (UV and impact), water sports (polarised). Dispensing choices: lens type, frame, coatings, filters, tints and prism.

decks.title: Occupational dispensing worksheets (with answers)
decks.summary: Five worksheets: occupations needing colour, VA or field standards; visual criteria for different jobs; occupational hazards; task analysis and driving standards; and using the nomogram. Answers are in 'Mgmt_AaD_12_Occupational Dispensing worksheet answers_EH.pptx'; the main ones are in the occupational dispensing topic.
takeaways: Crane drivers need depth perception and good peripheral fields; interior designers and decorators need colour discrimination.
Welders risk arc eye (photokeratitis); cement dust is alkaline.

decks.title: Cataract
decks.summary: The crystalline lens from embryology to ageing (anatomy, composition, transparency, UV absorption, accommodation), then cataract: symptoms, when to refer, risk factors, types and classification, paediatric cataract, and how surgery developed from couching to phacoemulsification.
takeaways: The lens is about 10 mm wide and 4 mm thick, about 15 D (a third of the eye's power), 64% water and 35% protein, with index 1.38 (cortex) to 1.40 (nucleus).
It absorbs UV from 300 to 400 nm; yellowing with age protects the retina.
Symptoms: myopic shift, gradually worsening vision (worse in bright light), glare, monocular diplopia and haloes.
Refer when cataract limits quality of life, work, driving (whatever the Snellen acuity) and the patient wants surgery.
Types: cortical (most common), nuclear, posterior subcapsular (steroids, uveitis). UK surgery is now almost all day-case phaco.

outline.title: Lens anatomy and composition
points: Lens placode at 3 weeks, vesicle at 6 weeks; tunica vasculosa lentis regresses before birth.
Capsule, single-layer anterior epithelium, zonules, and 2,100–2,300 hexagonal fibres laid down throughout life, meeting at Y sutures.
Transparency comes from a highly ordered structure; a healthy lens scatters about 5% of light.

outline.title: Optics, accommodation and ageing
points: Lens UV absorption (300–400 nm) creates pigments that yellow it; it fluoresces in UV.
Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonules so the lens rounds up (anterior surface most).
With age the lens gets heavier (100 mg at birth, 250 mg at 65), flatter, less deformable and more yellow. Extra risks: UV, smoking, dehydration, steroids, diabetes, uveitis.

outline.title: Cataract
points: Any lens opacity; WHO estimates 20 million blind from cataract, the commonest cause of blindness.
Risk factors: cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal and gut disease, smoking, hypertension, low socio-economic status, low antioxidants.
Cortical 63%, nuclear 41%, posterior subcapsular 24% (30% mixed). Paediatric: IOLs from about 4 weeks, left hyperopic, occlusion if one eye is done first.

outline.title: Surgery
points: About 400,000 NHS operations a year; outcomes have improved from 6/60 to a third reaching 6/12 or better.
Couching, then intracapsular and extracapsular extraction, small-incision surgery and phacoemulsification.
Anaesthesia: topical, peribulbar or general. Phaco: an ultrasonic probe emulsifies the nucleus, the posterior capsule supports the IOL, self-sealing small incisions, recovery 4–6 weeks.

decks.title: Automated refraction
decks.summary: How autorefractors work, how they're used in practice and research, photorefraction, their limitations (instrument myopia, pupil size, media opacities), open- versus closed-field designs, and how they're evaluated against subjective refraction.
takeaways: Autorefractors analyse infrared light reflected from the fundus to find the far point, with minimal patient input.
In practice they give a starting point for subjective refraction (as do retinoscopy, old records and focimetry) and often measure K readings too.
Main problem: proximal accommodation (instrument myopia); fogging targets help relax it.
Minimum pupil about 2.0–2.9 mm depending on instrument; some can't measure through cataract (SLD sources do better than LEDs).
Compare cylinders with vector components: MSE = sphere + cyl/2, J0 = −C cos2θ/2, J45 = −C sin2θ/2.

outline.title: Objective and automated refraction
points: Objective: no subjective response needed; retinoscopy, simple optometers or autorefractors.
Older manual instruments (Fincham, Rodenstock) to modern ones (Huvitz, Topcon, Nidek).
Often run by optical assistants.

outline.title: Photorefraction and limitations
points: Photorefractors (e.g. Plusoptix) analyse the light pattern reflected through the pupil: useful for screening children.
Range about ±25 D; minimum pupil about 2.0 mm (Topcon, Nidek, Huvitz) up to 2.9 mm.
Practice instruments are closed-field; research instruments are open-field (a natural view, less proximal accommodation).

outline.title: Clinical evaluation
points: Gibson and Davies (2008) evaluated the Nidek ARK-530A in 65 adults against subjective refraction.
Use MSE, J0 and J45 to compare cylinders; Bland-Altman plots show agreement and repeatability (difference against mean).

decks.title: Soft contact lens materials, manufacture and selection
decks.file: Mgmt_CLB_12_Soft CL materials manufacture and selection_DD -no vioceover.pptx
decks.summary: The ideal soft lens material, oxygen supply to the cornea, permeability, transmissibility and how they're measured, the corneal effects of hypoxia, wettability tests, contact lens optics, and hydrogel versus silicone hydrogel chemistry and complications.
takeaways: Corneal oxygen comes from the air (open eye), the palpebral conjunctiva (closed eye), the limbus and the aqueous.
Holden-Mertz: Dk/t of 24 (EOP 9.9%) for daily wear and 87 (EOP 17.9%) for extended wear to avoid swelling; later estimates are higher (35 and 125, or 175).
Hypoxia causes microcysts, oedema, endothelial blebs and polymegethism, lower corneal pH and neovascularisation; the cornea swells 3–4% overnight even without lenses.
Silicone hydrogels separate oxygen and water pathways, removing hypoxic complications, but MK rates are unchanged and mucin balls can occur.
Wettability: sessile drop, Wilhelmy plate, captive bubble (where advancing and receding angles reverse).

outline.title: Oxygen
points: Ideal material: oxygen, inert, wettable, spoilage-resistant, biocompatible, stable, durable, clear, low-maintenance, easy to make.
Dk measured at 34°C; the original Fatt method overestimates (boundary and edge effects): corrected values are about 25% lower, coulometric 5–10% lower again. EOP varies with method.
Signs of low Dk/t: microcysts, polymegethism, lower pH, oedema, blebs.

outline.title: Wettability and optics
points: Sessile drop: under 90° is more wettable. Wilhelmy plate: advancing and receding angles. Captive bubble: the reverse.
Poor wetting means worse vision, more deposits, discomfort and a home for microbes.
Indices and BVP and vertex distance formulae (recap).

outline.title: Hydrogel versus silicone hydrogel
points: Normal oxygen 21% open eye, 8% closed; problems start below about 13% (mitosis), 10% (lactate) and 8% (sensitivity).
Hydrogel Dk rises with water content but can't reach extended wear needs; silicone hydrogels (surface-treated, internal wetting, non-TRIS, water gradient) can.

Hydrogels like etafilcon A still give a quiet eye with low inflammation (lysozyme uptake). Silicone hydrogels: no hypoxia, more mechanical events in early generations, mucin balls; CIEs and MK unchanged when modality is matched.

decks.title: Adverse reactions 2
decks.summary: Ocular reactions to systemic drugs (amiodarone, vigabatrin, corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, tamoxifen and vortex keratopathy) and adverse reactions to the topical drugs optometrists use (cycloplegics, mydriatics, anaesthetics and chloramphenicol).
takeaways: Amiodarone: corneal microdeposits (common, reversible), night glare, optic neuropathy.
Vigabatrin: field constriction in about 30%, dose-dependent and irreversible.
Steroids: posterior subcapsular cataract and raised IOP. Hydroxychloroquine: bull's eye maculopathy (1–2%). Tamoxifen: retinopathy, keratopathy, PSC.
Cyclopentolate 1% can cause systemic effects in up to 10% after repeated doses (tachycardia, hallucinations, ataxia); tropicamide's main ocular risk is angle closure.
Topical anaesthetics: the main ocular reaction is corneal desquamation; avoid repeat doses and rubbing, and no contact lenses for 25 minutes.

outline.title: Systemic drugs
points: Patients on these drugs often need more frequent checks.
Amiodarone deposits appear within about 3 months, don't stain and clear 3–7 months after stopping.
Vortex keratopathy (verticillata): amiodarone, chloroquine, tamoxifen, chlorpromazine, indometacin.

outline.title: Cycloplegics and mydriatics
points: Cyclopentolate, tropicamide, atropine, homatropine; watch patients after instillation.
Tropicamide systemic effects: dry mouth, tachycardia, headache, nausea, pallor, allergy. Signs of angle closure: severe pain, redness, haloes, headache, vomiting, corneal oedema.
Atropine poisoning: dry mouth and throat, difficulty swallowing, hot dry flushed skin, fast pulse; seek emergency advice.

outline.title: Anaesthetics and chloramphenicol
points: Anaesthetics: stinging and redness most common; slow epithelial healing, reduce tears and oxygen uptake; systemic lightheadedness, tinnitus, fainting.
Desquamation causes a sudden drop to about 6/60 with heavy staining.
Chloramphenicol: rare aplastic anaemia; avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and neonates (grey baby syndrome).
